articles.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
articles.body:
Russia's new suspected radar in Kaliningrad could spy deep into Europe
November 1, 2026
The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.
From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.
While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.
The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.
"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.
Mass surveillance system
The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.
"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.
"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."
Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.
"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.
Electronic warfare hub
The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.
"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.
"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.
Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.
The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.
"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.
ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.
Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.
"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."
This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."
Motivation for the West
She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.
"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."
Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.
In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.
The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.
Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

articles.title: Ukrainian air alert app hacked with fake nuclear warnings
articles.body:
Ukrainian air alert app hacked with fake nuclear warnings
Ukraine’s government-backed mobile air alert app sent out false warnings of nuclear and chemical attacks on Sunday night, Ukrainian media reported.
At around 11pm, the Air Alert app sent notifications urging residents to seek shelter due to a “radiation threat” and a “chemical attack.” It also warned of “street battles” in Kiev.
According to screenshots shared by Ukrainian media, one of the messages read in Russian: “Don’t worry, Oreshnik is coming,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile.
The Ukrainian Air Force urged residents to rely only on official sources. “The Air Alert app may have been compromised by hostile actors. There is no radiation threat!” it said in a brief statement on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry later confirmed that the app had been temporarily disabled following a suspected cyberattack.
According to Russian Telegram news channel Mash, a hacker group calling itself Hitcore claimed responsibility for the intrusion. Mash reported that the hackers said they had tricked an employee of a Ukrainian company into giving them access to his computer.
Although Mash described the hackers as Russian, the group has not previously been linked to any known cyberattacks. Moscow has consistently denied allegations of involvement in such operations.
About three hours later, the Russian Emergencies Ministry said its mobile app had also been hacked and used to send “false information” to users. The ministry said it was working to restore normal operations.
The incident came days after an apparent glitch in Kiev’s automated air alert system on October 26, when air raid warnings were issued and canceled several times within just five minutes. Officials blamed a “technical malfunction” and apologized for the disruption.
Ukraine has stepped up requests for additional air defense interceptors from the US and its European partners in recent months as its own defenses have struggled to counter Russian missile barrages and jet-powered drones.
Relations with Washington have become strained, however, as Kiev has refused to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which US President Donald Trump has blamed for soaring fuel prices, and criticized his decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Ukraine was also caught off guard by sudden disruptions to Starlink and Starshield satellite services widely used by its military, which officials in Kiev linked to US efforts to pressure Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky.

articles.title: Iran pursues expanded deterrence strategy, calls for new regional security order
articles.body:
Iran pursues expanded deterrence strategy, calls for new regional security order
TEHRAN – Iran's military and political leadership has outlined a broader strategy for confronting potential threats, combining expanded military preparedness, a wider operational theater, stronger deterrence capabilities, and diplomatic efforts to establish a regional security framework independent of outside powers.
The strategy follows a series of directives issued by Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei during a meeting with senior Armed Forces commanders. The instructions emphasize intelligent combat readiness, an immediate and effective response to threats without geographical restrictions, stronger military intelligence and the development of indigenous defense capabilities.
 
Senior Iranian officials have subsequently elaborated on different dimensions of the strategy, addressing military preparedness, the future of Iran's nuclear doctrine, the Strait of Hormuz, regional security cooperation and the international economic consequences of the conflict.
Expanded operational theater and new military targets
 
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), announced that identifying new targets and planning operations across additional geographical areas had been placed on the Corps' agenda.
Speaking in Kerman, Mohebbi said the process of identifying new targets and preparing operational plans for a broader geographical theater had begun two days earlier.
He described the Leader's latest directives as opening a new chapter in the confrontation, adding that Iran's Armed Forces were now better prepared to deliver an effective response to potential threats.
Mohebbi said the removal of geographical restrictions would provide Iran with a wider operational field to confront hostile actions and establish comprehensive deterrence.
He also recalled that the late Leader had previously emphasized the regionalization of any war against Iran, adding that the latest instructions had further expanded the geographical scope of the country's defensive planning.
The IRGC spokesperson said the ultimate objective was to establish maximum deterrence, making any attempt to threaten Iran's territorial integrity, national security, and interests prohibitively costly.
Armed forces enhancing readiness to counter complex threats
The Iranian Armed Forces are further strengthening their expertise and operational readiness to confront complex threats and hybrid warfare, the commander of the Iranian Navy has said.
Rear Admiral Shahram Irani made the remarks during a session of the War Studies course at Shahid Sattari University, according to Mehr News Agency.
He highlighted the 86th Naval Flotilla’s round-the-world voyage, describing it as the outcome of months of planning and specialized efforts by Navy personnel. Despite challenging oceanic conditions, he said, the mission was successfully completed, securing Iran’s place in the history of the country’s maritime navigation.
Irani also praised the capabilities and commitment of Navy personnel, saying the flotilla’s visits to ports in various countries provided an opportunity to showcase Iran’s Islamic and national identity.
He added that the crew’s professional conduct and adherence to religious and ethical values had demonstrated an aspect of the Islamic Republic of Iran’s capabilities and standing.
Emphasizing the importance of self-confidence, faith and hope in confronting threats, the naval commander said determination and perseverance, alongside faith and hope, were essential factors for success.
He stressed that the Armed Forces were drawing on these qualities to further enhance their knowledge and preparedness to deal with increasingly complex threats and hybrid warfare.
Five strategic setbacks for the United States
In assessing the consequences of the conflict, Mohebbi outlined five areas in which the United States had suffered strategic setbacks.
The first, he argued, concerned about Washington's failure to achieve its initial political and territorial objectives. According to the IRGC spokesperson, the United States had initially sought to change Iran's political system and fragment the country. After failing to achieve these objectives, it gradually shifted to demands involving Iran's missile capabilities, nuclear activities, enriched uranium, and control over strategic assets, including oil wells and islands.
Mohebbi maintained that none of these objectives had been achieved, arguing that the failure to accomplish the original goals had compelled Washington to reconsider its approach and seek negotiations and mediation.
The second setback concerned the credibility of the US security strategy in West Asia. He said Washington had justified its extensive military presence in the region by promising to protect energy supplies and freedom of navigation through major international waterways.
However, despite possessing what Mohebbi described as the world's largest navy, seven fleets, 12 aircraft carriers and a regional Fifth Fleet presence, the United States had been unable to reopen the Strait of Hormuz during the conflict.
He argued that this had raised fundamental questions about Washington's ability to guarantee maritime security and protect international energy flows.
The third setback concerned US intelligence capabilities. Mohebbi said the identification and targeting of American intelligence facilities had challenged the perception that US intelligence infrastructure and methods were beyond detection.
The fourth involved the perceived superiority of American military technology. He cited Iran's ability to counter advanced US military systems, including the F-35 fighter aircraft, Patriot missile systems, and other equipment operating in the air, underwater, and on land.
The fifth setback, he said, involved the economic costs of the conflict and the weakening of American global influence. Mohebbi argued that Washington, which had traditionally sought to transfer the financial burden of military campaigns to other countries, had itself sustained significant economic damage.
He also described the conflict as a challenge to the perception of US military invincibility and its ability to protect its allies.
Armed forces prepare for immediate and unrestricted responses
The military dimension of the new strategy was further emphasized by Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of the Iranian Armed Forces.
In a message published on his X account, Abdollahi said the Armed Forces were employing their full intelligence capabilities to monitor enemy movements and preparations while continuously updating their target database.
He stressed that Iran would not necessarily wait for an adversary to launch an attack before determining the timing and manner of its response.
"Our response will be immediate, impactful, and without geographical restrictions," he warned.
In a separate message addressed to the Iranian nation, Abdollahi praised the Leader's directives, describing them as a guiding framework for military commanders and all members of the Armed Forces.
He pledged that the military would stand firm against any aggression, regardless of its scale or nature, and defend the country and its people.
Abdollahi also said the Armed Forces were developing a new database of enemy targets and assets across a wider geographical area, adding that Iran would confront its adversaries with new operational capabilities.
Meanwhile, Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaqi pledged the Defense Ministry's full support for implementing the Leader's instructions.
He said the ministry would mobilize its organizational, industrial, scientific, and technological capacities to translate the directives into practical defense achievements, with particular emphasis on strengthening indigenous capabilities and meeting the requirements of the Armed Forces.
Nuclear doctrine remains unchanged amid growing debate
Iran's nuclear policy was another major issue addressed by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
Rezaei said no official decision had been taken to change the country's nuclear doctrine, stating that the issue could be discussed if military hostilities resumed.
Rezaei pointed out that Iran had accepted inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and maintained surveillance cameras at its nuclear facilities, with monitoring information transmitted to the agency.
He said the Iranian public was questioning why the country should continue with the same arrangements when its nuclear facilities had come under attack despite the existing inspection and monitoring framework.
The SNSC secretary added that some members of Parliament had apparently begun preliminary steps concerning the issue, but emphasized that no formal government or state-level decision had been adopted.
Rezaei also criticized IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, arguing that problems surrounding Iran's nuclear file had emerged during his tenure.
On the diplomatic front, he said Tehran was awaiting the latest response from Washington in the ongoing indirect exchanges. He added that he had read a letter from US Vice President JD Vance but had not yet sent a reply.
Describing the change in the American side's tone as a positive indication, Rezaei said it reflected Iran's strengthened position.
He reiterated that diplomacy remained an option, provided that the seven conditions previously announced by Iran were fulfilled. However, he warned that any renewed hostile action would be met with devastating strikes using new weapons.
Four-country consultations seek regional security without outside interference
Alongside its military preparations, Tehran has emphasized the importance of developing a regional security framework based on cooperation among West Asian countries.
Rezaei discussed the outcome of the four-country consultations in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, saying the participants had reached a constructive understanding of several shared regional priorities.
He said the discussions addressed the future security architecture of the region, the situation in Yemen, the proposed Mecca agreement and the need to defend Muslim populations against Israeli aggression.
The withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon and southern Syria, as well as developments in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, were also among the subjects discussed.
Rezaei argued that developments over the past one or two years had demonstrated that no sustainable regional security arrangement could be established without taking Iran's position and interests into account.
He said the resistance demonstrated by the Iranian nation had encouraged regional countries to reconsider their security policies and explore arrangements based on cooperation among countries of the region.
According to the SNSC secretary, the emerging framework should enable regional states to take responsibility for their own security without interference from powers outside the region.
He added that some regional officials who had visited Tehran to discuss future security arrangements had themselves requested meetings with Iranian officials.
Rezaei maintained that Iran's ability to withstand the military power of the United States and Israel demonstrated the potential of cooperation among regional countries to establish lasting security.
He stressed that Iran should have an effective role in any future regional security arrangement, arguing that sustainable stability could not be achieved without its participation.
Strait of Hormuz and national interests remain non-negotiable
The strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz also featured prominently in Rezaei's remarks.
He said reopening the waterway was conditional on the full implementation of Iran's requirements and that no change in its status would take place until those conditions were fulfilled.
The SNSC secretary stressed that Iran would not retreat from its rights and national interests during negotiations.
He added that any eventual conclusion to the conflict should ensure that no country would contemplate aggression against Iran in the future.
Economic consequences extend beyond the battlefield
Rezaei also addressed the wider economic consequences of the conflict, arguing that its impact had extended beyond West Asia and affected households and businesses in different parts of the world.
He cited rising energy, fuel, gasoline, and heating costs in the United States, saying that even relatively affluent households had experienced financial pressure.
According to Rezaei, the economic consequences of the conflict had not been limited to the United States or the immediate region but had affected living costs internationally.
Comparing the confrontation with the Vietnam War, he argued that the latest conflict had produced broader global economic repercussions.
He also referred to growing criticism of US President Donald Trump, attributing the dissatisfaction in part to the economic consequences of the military campaign.
Rezaei further pointed to a 'shift in the positions of European leaders,' saying that French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had initially welcomed the US military campaign but were now expressing concern about its economic repercussions.
He maintained that national security remained a non-negotiable priority for Iran and that the economic difficulties experienced by the Iranian people should be considered alongside the country's longer-term strategic objectives.
Acknowledging the hardships imposed on households, Rezaei said the achievements of national resistance and the prospects it offered future generations outweighed the economic difficulties.
He also warned that any further hostile action would be met with a powerful response, expressing confidence that Iran would emerge from the current period with its national dignity and security preserved.
A strategy combining defense, diplomacy and regional cooperation
The statements by Iran's military and political leadership indicate an approach that combines expanded defense preparedness with diplomatic engagement and efforts to strengthen regional cooperation.
The central element of the strategy is the establishment of 'maximum deterrence: strengthening military and intelligence capabilities, broadening operational preparedness and ensuring that any potential aggression carries consequences sufficient to discourage its repetition.'
At the diplomatic level, Tehran continues to emphasize the fulfillment of its conditions, the protection of national interests, and the need for a regional security framework based on the participation of neighboring countries.
Together, these positions reflect Iran's stated determination to strengthen its defensive capabilities while pursuing a regional order in which security is primarily the responsibility of the countries of the region.

articles.title: India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
articles.body:
India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Despite India’s increased defense spending, robust government support for domestic arms and military technology manufacturers, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal focus on the development of the military-industrial complex, experts warn that the Indian Air Force faces a critical squadron decline that may influence its ability to counter potential adversaries.
This paradox stems from India’s procurement policies, which do not prioritize the acquisition of advanced aircraft for the air force. Apparently, segments of India’s business elite and military leadership, possibly influenced by Western companies, are lobbying for contracts that offer questionable benefits to the country’s armed forces.
While India’s geopolitical and military rivals (China and Pakistan) invest in cutting-edge technology – such as the fifth-generation J-20 and J-35 multi-role fighters – India continues to acquire fourth-generation aircraft like the Rafale and Tejas fighters. However, such aircraft cannot address modern combat challenges or threats effectively.
The situation looks even more dire considering that the Rafale and Tejas fighters are not superior to the Su-30MKI, the primary fighter in service with the Indian Air Force, and may even fall short when it comes to certain tactical specifications. The Su-30MKI boasts significant advantages in speed, maneuverability, payload capacity, and operational range.
This raises a crucial question: why are substantial financial resources from the Indian budget allocated for the purchase of expensive aircraft (Rafale fighters cost about €160 million each) directly from the French private firm Dassault Aviation, when the state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) offers the option to procure Su-30MKI aircraft assembled under license from Russia at a considerably lower cost?
Real threats
Clearly, the rivalry between Pakistan (and China, which stands behind it) and India is not going to fade anytime soon. In fact, competition will likely intensify in the foreseeable future. A critical factor in preventing the most dangerous scenarios lies in maintaining a balance of military capabilities and defense potential between the opposing sides. So, what does the power balance look like today?
Islamabad and Beijing are heavily investing in fifth-generation multirole fighters. By 2030, Pakistan is expected to field no fewer than 40 J-35AE fighters, while the Chinese Air Force could deploy up to 500 J-20s and J-35 fighters. Additionally, the Chinese Navy may have over 50 carrier-based J-35s. In total, this amounts to about 600 fifth-generation fighters – each one of them superior to any fourth-generation aircraft.
Armed with highly effective long-range air-to-air weapons, Pakistan and China’s stealthy fifth-generation fighters will be able to launch missile attacks without being detected by Indian Air Force radar systems. Under such circumstances, India’s military aviation could face a devastating defeat, leading to humiliation and a prolonged recovery process. This is inevitable, since fifth-generation fighters surpass fourth-generation aircraft.
The strategy of overwhelming the enemy with sheer numbers and concentrating an extensive air force over specific combat zones, is fundamentally flawed: no number of Rafale or Tejas fighters can match the combat capabilities of J-20 and J-35 aircraft.
The air forces of Pakistan and China possess cutting-edge technologies like stealth capabilities, advanced radar systems capable of covertly tracking opponents, and long-range missiles that significantly outdistance those in the arsenals of Rafale and Tejas fighters.
However, if the Indian Air Force were to acquire Su-57E fighters, equipped with stealth technology, the modern N-036 Byelka radar, long-range RVV-BD missiles, and other state-of-the-art munitions, India’s ability to confront its neighbors in the above-mentioned scenarios would change dramatically.
Why Russia?
For over 70 years, Soviet and Russian aviation technology has been in service with the Indian military, demonstrating remarkable efficiency and reliability. Russia has proven to be a dependable partner in military-technical cooperation.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has praised the quality and effectiveness of Russian weapons, particularly highlighting their successful deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Moscow is eager to continue the mutually beneficial collaboration with New Delhi in the defense sector. This includes maintaining the joint Su-30MKI program and potentially organizing licensed assembly of the fifth-generation Su-57E fighter at facilities operated by India’s HAL.
The ongoing modernization of the Pakistani Air Force and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force with advanced aircraft has prompted India to take decisive actions to restore parity and the balance of power. Given the current circumstances, a swift acquisition of 50 Su-57E fighters from Russia under a fast-track mechanism, along with plans for licensed production of an additional 450 units in India, seems like the most prudent course of action. This could involve the latest two-seat variant, the Su-57D. Over the next few decades, such a project would effectively address the challenges and threats that India faces.
More than just a prototype
The Su-57 fighter jet has already entered service with the Russian Air Force and has participated in combat operations.
India contributed to the development of the fighter that served as the basis for the Su-57. In 2010, the Indian Ministry of Defense initiated the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program to create an indigenous fifth-generation fighter. However, after more than 15 years, this program has yet to reach the flight testing stage. Serial production is not likely to commence before 2035.
Alexander Mikheev, head of Rosoboronexport, and Vadim Badekha, head of the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), confirmed that the Su-57 aircraft – specifically its export version, the Su-57E – is already being delivered abroad. The Su-57E is available for friendly countries collaborating with Russia on defense projects. If India approaches Moscow regarding the supply of this combat aircraft, Russia would likely respond in a positive manner.
Moreover, advanced Russian technologies transferred to India under a licensing agreement will assist Indian specialists in refining and successfully implementing several national projects, including the AMCA.
Unlike American F-35s – which have struggled to maintain supersonic speeds in sustained cruise mode – the Su-57 meets all the criteria expected of a fifth-generation fighter.
For New Delhi, the Su-57 offers multiple advantages, especially since it was designed at the same bureau that developed the Su-30MKI – the Indian Air Force’s primary combat aircraft as of 2026. This continuity provides valuable benefits in terms of operational procedures, maintenance, repair, and logistical support, leveraging existing airfield, storage, and training infrastructures.
Indigenous programs
Prime Minister Narendra Modi highly supports India’s national defense industry initiatives. He made history as the first prime minister of India to fly in the cockpit of a supersonic fighter jet.
Professional pilots who have flown the Tejas aircraft praise its performance, noting it surpasses the MiG-21, which the Tejas was designed to replace under the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) program that began in 1983. However, the mission was not fulfilled; the project has faced significant delays, and by the time the Tejas was deployed in 2015, the vast majority of the 874 MiG-21s acquired by the Indian Air Force between 1963 and 1987 had already been retired due to wear and tear. Instead of 20 squadrons of MiG aircraft, by 2026, the Indian Air Force had just two Tejas squadrons consisting of 30 single-seat and six two-seat models. Field tests are being conducted to identify and rectify issues on aircraft from the initial production batch.
The 18th Squadron, formed in 2020, has already lost two Tejas planes in accidents – one in March 2024 and another in November 2025. The latter incident involved a fatal failure during a demonstration flight at an airshow in Dubai. The initial variant (Mark I) will no longer be produced, as it proved unreliable and technically inadequate.
Like many Indian projects, Tejas is plagued by delays which result in technological obsolescence by the time of production. Consequently, the substantial financial investments in such programs fail to deliver the expected returns or strengthen India’s defense capabilities.
Indian manufacturers also developed a naval version of the Tejas. Testing began in 2020 aboard the INS Vikramaditya aircraft carrier (built by Russia under Project 11430) and continued three years later on the indigenously constructed INS Vikrant. The compact design of the Tejas offers advantages for hangar storage; however, with a standard combat load, it can only operate within a few hundred miles. During combat operations, the carrier would need to approach the target closer, increasing the risk of retaliatory strikes from the enemy.
After conducting evaluations, the Indian Navy concluded that such an aircraft was not suitable for carrier operations. The official reason for rejecting the LCA-Navy was its low thrust-to-weight ratio, which prevented full utilization of the aircraft’s potential when taking off from an aircraft carrier. In response to requests from Indian industry, further tests were conducted on an upgraded version, but its performance still fell short of naval requirements.
Coming to terms with the LCA-Navy’s inability to meet expectations, Indian aerospace engineers proposed a completely new aircraft – the Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF), which bears a striking resemblance to the French Rafale-M. This move signifies a concession by the creators and advocates of the Tejas, acknowledging their defeat in the competition for carrier aviation. Work on the TEDBF began in 2020. The prototype’s first flight is scheduled for 2032 and serial production is anticipated in 2038.
Meanwhile, last year, the People’s Liberation Army Navy received its third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, equipped with fifth-generation J-35 fighters. Construction has also begun on the fourth Type 004 aircraft carrier. It will likely have a displacement of around 100,000 tons and accommodate an air wing of 100 aircraft, including the J-35.
Dependence on the US
In coordination with the main contractor, Indian industry continues Tejas Mark IA testing, which started in spring 2022. Without waiting for these trials to conclude, the Indian Air Force has placed two successive orders totaling 141 single-seat and 41 two-seat aircraft, scheduled for delivery between 2027 and 2032. Production will take place at two facilities in Bangalore and Nasik.
Following this, production of the Tejas Mark II is expected to commence. The first test flight has faced multiple delays and is now expected no earlier than 2028. While no firm order has been placed for this new model, the Air Force leadership hopes to eventually have 18 squadrons of Tejas aircraft, including 10 Mark II variant squadrons.
The idea to direct resources into producing fourth-generation fighters for the next decade seems imprudent, given that China has mastered mass production of fifth-generation aircraft and is set to begin transitioning to sixth-generation models in the coming years. Deliveries of Chinese J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan are underway, while existing JF-17s are being upgraded with systems and munitions developed for the J-35.
However, a far more pressing issue is the potential deepening dependence on the United States. Throughout the practical implementation of the LCA program, the technical specifications of the aircraft have been repeatedly adjusted, primarily by replacing certain Indian components with foreign ones, which gradually increases the foreign share in the cost of mass-produced products. Among the imported items, the most expensive was the US engine, which had to replace the GTX-35VS Kaveri engine which faced challenges in meeting technical criteria.
Negotiations for a licensed production agreement for the F414 engine have been challenging, largely because Washington is reluctant to share advanced General Electric technologies developed with Pentagon funding. The US is only willing to share some of the technology, omitting the most sensitive components.
The reluctance to fully share F414 engine technology can be explained by one factor: Washington seeks to maintain leverage over New Delhi by controlling the pace of the licensed production of engines for India’s frontline air force.
The second most costly imported component is the onboard radar system. Development of an indigenous MMR radar was halted due to unsatisfactory test results, leading to a preference for foreign alternatives. The prototype aircraft utilized the Ericsson-Ferranti PS-05 radar, originally designed for the Swedish JAS-39 Gripen. Delays in the LCA program rendered the PS-05 obsolete, resulting in its discontinuation. It has since been replaced by the EL/M-2032, which now equips Mark I variants.
It’s worth noting that Elta’s product is also outdated; it was developed in the 1980s for the Israeli Lavi fighter jet (canceled in 1987). The obsolescence is particularly evident in its use of mechanical beam scanning, while the Russian N-011M radar on the Su-30MKI, which was introduced into the Indian Air Force in 2002, boasts more advanced electronic scanning technology.
Recently, Elta proposed the EL/M-2052 with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar configuration. The manufacturer promises to refine it by the time Mark IA aircraft (formed in 2015) are delivered to the air force, projected for late this year or early next year. Various publications have diligently presented Israeli radars as a “temporary solution” for the Tejas program, but as seen with General Electric engines, “temporary” solutions often end up being used much longer than expected.
Strategic decision-making
The practical implementation of the LCA program has resulted in yet another fourth-generation supersonic fighter jet emerging on the global stage. However, the Tejas does not surpass its foreign counterparts. Technically, the Tejas Mark I barely matches the Chinese FC-1, which was adopted by the Pakistan Air Force as the JF-17 in 2007. At best, the Tejas Mark II might reach the level of the JF-17 Block III (with AESA, operational since 2023) and the J-10CE, which Pakistani pilots effectively utilized to fend off an Indian airstrike in May 2025.
With the Indian Air Force already operating a substantial fleet of over 300 Su-30MKIs and Rafale aircraft, which are far better suited for the interception of aerial threats and air superiority missions, the Tejas Mark I may only serve effectively in ground attack operations and pilot training. Fortunately, being a lightweight, single-engine aircraft means it has low fuel consumption. Nevertheless, its limited thrust-to-weight ratio, outdated radar, reduced payload capacity, and narrow selection of munitions (lacking long-range air-to-air missiles), along with the absence of critical stealth technologies naturally confine the aircraft to its own niche. The Su-57E is in a different class altogether.
Consequently, the Tejas cannot be viewed as a viable alternative to the Su-57E. Continuing the LCA program in its current form hampers the decision-making process, since the program competes for budget resources. Moreover, there’s another contender for state funding – the AMCA, with its first flight planned for 2034 and serial production slated for 2036.
In selecting a fifth-generation fighter program, decision-makers in India will need to consider numerous factors and criteria that can sometimes be conflicting and contradictory. Among these is the inherent bias towards domestic projects (i.e. AMCA, LCA, etc.), even if they may not be technically or technologically superior compared to the best foreign alternatives.
The desire to produce everything domestically is understandable, but there are many compelling arguments in favor of purchasing the best foreign technologies or producing them under license. The advanced Su-57E, a premier frontline fighter, is one of such example. For India, Russia remains a reliable partner as decades of effective military-technical collaboration have proven.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Give Us Patriot Missiles, We'll Stop Strikes On Russian Refineries
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would cease strikes on Russian oil refineries -- as demanded by US President Donald Trump -- if the US would quickly provide Kyiv with Patriot air-defense missiles.
Zelensky, in an interview with Fox News on November 1, said he had conducted "different and several" discussions with the US president and his aides on the matter.
"We [said] we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he told host Trey Yingst.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles. We will find money; [it's] not just aid...We will pay for it."
Zelensky said if the US provided the missile systems for one month, Ukraine would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same amount of time.
Could Take 'Several Years'
The US State Department on October 30 announced the approval of a critically needed sale of Patriot air defense interceptors to Ukraine worth $2.1 billion to strengthen Kyiv’s defenses against increasing Russian aerial attacks.
Zelenskyy, however, has warned that the 500 missile interceptors could take “several years” to arrive.
Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that “500 PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number” and could form an effective defense package this winter, but he added that “deliveries may begin only in a few years.”
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said.

articles.body:

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said two oil tankers "exploded" after striking mines while traveling through an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported on Sunday.
Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels seeking to pass through the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked ships it says violate those restrictions, as it seeks to assert control over the strategic waterway and exert pressure on the US.
US President Donald Trump held a call with Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu over when and whether to ramp up combat operations against Iran, US media reported Sunday.

The Israeli source described the call as "tough," while the American source said it was "direct," according to Axios.

The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.

In a statement, the internal security forces announced the arrest of "two individuals following close intelligence surveillance" in Deir Ezzor.
They are accused of "carrying out a series of assassinations in the governorate, the latest of which was targeting Ministry of Defence member Ibrahim al-Jassem" in the city of Mayadin.
Houthi media said on Sunday that Saudi airstrikes targeted a key Red Sea port in Hodeidah province, as the Iran-backed group battles a Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government.

The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the United States while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said on Sunday, following threats of a resumption of the Middle East war.
"We're hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough," diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round...But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.

"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Iran's supreme leader warned the United States and Israel on Saturday of fresh attacks following their threats to resume strikes after crucial elections, as fears increased over a return to fighting.
President Donald Trump suggested he could launch fresh military action after the United States holds its midterm elections early next week.
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday: "If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it."
A Yemeni staff member of the UN Human Rights Office has died in Houthi custody after being arbitrarily detained for more than two years, the UN human rights chief said on Saturday, calling for an independent investigation and the release of other detained personnel.
Mohammad el Shami had been held by the Houthi militant group since June 6, 2024, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said in a statement.
His family said they had been informed of his death only recently, more than a month after it occurred, and had received no explanation of the cause or circumstances, Turk said.
A Qatari tanker has been attacked with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters, the country's state news agency reported Sunday.
The attack on Friday evening struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, owned by the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war broke out in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.
