In a statement, the internal security forces announced the arrest of "two individuals following close intelligence surveillance" in Deir Ezzor.
They are accused of "carrying out a series of assassinations in the governorate, the latest of which was targeting Ministry of Defence member Ibrahim al-Jassem" in the city of Mayadin.
Houthi media said on Sunday that Saudi airstrikes targeted a key Red Sea port in Hodeidah province, as the Iran-backed group battles a Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government.
"The Saudi enemy has launched two airstrikes on Ras Issa port," Al-Masirah TV said, subsequently adding that Saudi Arabia had attacked the "pier and a commercial ship there in a series of airstrikes".
Hodeidah has the biggest seaport under Houthi control and is a key entry point for food and aid to areas they hold. The Ras Issa port, north of the city, also serves to import and store oil.
Houthi media on Sunday also reported strikes targeting the faculty of medicine at Hodeidah University, in the same province, while two residents told AFP they heard an explosion in the area.
The Saudi-led coalition, for its part, said it had conducted "a precision operation to neutralise vital resources" used by the Houthis.
The head of Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Sunday that an ongoing investigation into alleged foreign funding in the country's recent vote would not invalidate its result, noting that so far "suspicions remain suspicions".
"We will examine them thoroughly and get to the very bottom of the matter in order to establish the full truth," committee chief Noam Sohlberg said in a video message. "Our position is that even if the suspicions are ultimately confirmed, this would not call into question the integrity of the electoral process or the overall results of the elections."
Somali pirates have seized an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 23 people, the Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean said, warning that the ship was approaching a commercial shipping lane and could become a floating base for further attacks.
The Azini was hijacked Thursday between the coastal towns of Bandar Bayla and Hafun in northeastern Somalia, a maritime security officer with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said Sunday.
The officer told The Associated Press that 12 pirates seized the vessel, which was carrying 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorised to speak with the media.
The centre said the crew’s safety was unknown in an alert dated Saturday. In an updated warning, it said that pirates could use the vessel as a “mother ship” to support attacks on commercial vessels.
Houthi media, citing an anonymous military official, renewed threats on Sunday against Saudi oil giant Aramco and aviation in the kingdom.
Yemen's Houthis, fighting a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government, are allies of Iran, which on Sunday warned the US and Israel not to renew strikes on the Islamic Republic after they had threatened a return to war.
"Aramco facilities are within range of the Yemeni Armed Forces, and investments in them are a venture fraught with losses," the Houthis' Saba news agency quoted the military official as saying.
The official also warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace "except for the airspaces of Mecca and Medina".
Almost all were displaced in the last two months, and they "urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care", the International Organisation for Migration said in a statement.
British police said Sunday they had arrested 325 people at a London protest in support of Palestine Action the previous day, ahead of a court appeal over the government's contentious ban of the group.
Demonstrators staged a "mass action" outside the US embassy ahead of the Supreme Court holding a two-day hearing from Wednesday on the UK government's July 2025 decision to outlaw Palestine Action under anti-terror legislation.
It has resulted in more than 4,000 people, including many senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, being arrested for showing their support for the group, according to campaigners and police tallies.
"In total, 325 people were arrested yesterday," London's Metropolitan Police said in an update Sunday.
"The vast majority of arrests, 320, were for expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act."
Yamaha said on Sunday it won't participate in next weekend's Qatar MotoGP, citing "the situation in the Middle East".
"Yamaha has not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions," the Japanese manufacturer said.
Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the 3 November US midterm elections. President Donald Trump has said the United States will not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action thereafter.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East.
Five people were killed in Khan Yunis and three in Gaza City, according to a statement from the territory's civil defence service, which operates under the authority of the Islamist movement Hamas that runs Gaza.o
The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the United States while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said on Sunday, following threats of a resumption of the Middle East war.
"We're hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough," diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round...But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran's military but still has to "take care of" one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the United States and Israel in February, were "going fine but you know they're not very reliable."
The Republican president said the United States is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Iran's supreme leader warned the United States and Israel on Saturday of fresh attacks following their threats to resume strikes after crucial elections, as fears increased over a return to fighting.
President Donald Trump suggested he could launch fresh military action after the United States holds its midterm elections early next week.
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday: "If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it."
A Yemeni staff member of the UN Human Rights Office has died in Houthi custody after being arbitrarily detained for more than two years, the UN human rights chief said on Saturday, calling for an independent investigation and the release of other detained personnel.
Mohammad el Shami had been held by the Houthi militant group since June 6, 2024, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said in a statement.
His family said they had been informed of his death only recently, more than a month after it occurred, and had received no explanation of the cause or circumstances, Turk said.
A Qatari tanker has been attacked with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters, the country's state news agency reported Sunday.
The attack on Friday evening struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, owned by the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war broke out in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.

articles.title: Good Nuclear, Bad Nuclear
articles.body:
Good Nuclear, Bad Nuclear
Europe's nuclear hypocrisy: Why is Iran expected to remain defenceless?
TEHRAN- After decades of lecturing Iran over its nuclear programme, European powers are embracing nuclear deterrence, participating in simulated nuclear warfare and even contemplating the development of their own atomic weapons. The question is no longer simply whether Iran's nuclear programme is peaceful, but why the rules of international security appear to apply differently to Tehran and European capitals.
For decades, European governments have positioned themselves as guardians of nuclear non-proliferation, repeatedly questioning Iran's nuclear ambitions, imposing political and economic pressure, and demanding restrictions on its nuclear programme. Yet, as Europe increasingly prepares for a potential nuclear confrontation and considers expanding its own nuclear capabilities, an uncomfortable question emerges: by what logic can European countries claim the right to pursue nuclear deterrence while denying Iran the right to determine the means of safeguarding its own security?
A recent report by "German Foreign Policy", published on October 15 under the headline "Europe, a nuclear-armed continent", offers a revealing account of this apparent contradiction. It describes an accelerating trend towards the militarisation of Europe's security architecture, including participation in nuclear warfare exercises, discussions about deploying additional American nuclear weapons on European soil, and renewed calls for Germany and other European countries to consider developing their own nuclear weapons.
The developments expose not only Europe's changing security priorities but also the profound double standards underpinning its longstanding approach to Iran's nuclear programme.
The hypocrisy of Europe's nuclear double standards
For years, European governments have been at the forefront of international efforts to restrict Iran's nuclear programme, frequently invoking concerns that Tehran might eventually seek to develop nuclear weapons. These accusations have provided political justification for sanctions, diplomatic pressure and repeated attempts to impose additional restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities.
Yet the same European capitals are now moving in a remarkably different direction when it comes to their own nuclear ambitions.
According to German Foreign Policy, Germany is participating in NATO's annual Steadfast Noon nuclear warfare exercise, alongside 16 other NATO members. The exercise involves operational preparations for the simulated deployment of nuclear bombs. The Bundeswehr is also participating for the first time in France's nuclear exercise, Operation Poker.
Meanwhile, Finland has moved to remove its longstanding legal prohibition on hosting or transporting nuclear weapons, while Lithuania is pursuing a similar constitutional change. Discussions about potentially stationing American nuclear weapons in Poland have also gained momentum.
 
Perhaps even more significant is the growing debate over an independent European nuclear weapons capability. German foreign policy circles have begun openly discussing the possibility of a German or jointly developed European nuclear arsenal, potentially involving Scandinavian and Baltic countries.
The contrast is striking. When Iran develops its nuclear technology under international safeguards, European governments portray it as a potential threat to international security. When European countries expand their nuclear military cooperation and contemplate acquiring additional nuclear capabilities, the same developments are presented as legitimate responses to security concerns.
If nuclear capabilities are inherently destabilising when pursued by Iran, why do they suddenly become instruments of stability when pursued by European countries?
Security for Europe, insecurity for Iran?
The underlying contradiction goes beyond nuclear policy. It reflects a broader European understanding of international security in which some countries are considered entitled to strengthen their deterrence capabilities, while others are expected to accept limitations on their security choices.
French President Emmanuel Macron's declaration in March that Europe was entering a new "age of nuclear weapons" is particularly revealing. His proposed advanced deterrence concept involves the possible temporary deployment of French nuclear-capable Rafale aircraft at bases in other European countries. The objective, according to the report, is to create uncertainty for potential adversaries and complicate their military calculations.
In other words, Europe increasingly views nuclear deterrence as an essential component of its security.
Germany, meanwhile, is questioning whether dependence on American nuclear protection is sufficient. Political scientist Joachim Krause, a former head of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, has argued that Germany should consider its own or European nuclear weapons. He has even suggested that possessing an atomic bomb would provide Germany with an additional element of security.
This raises a fundamental question: if nuclear deterrence is considered necessary for Germany's protection, why should Iran be expected to surrender every option that could contribute to its national security?
Iran operates in a considerably more volatile security environment than most European countries. It faces decades of American sanctions, persistent military threats, repeated acts of sabotage, assassinations of its officials and scientists, and direct military attacks involving the United States and Israel. Its geographical neighbourhood is also characterised by extensive foreign military deployments and the presence of nuclear-armed states.
These are not abstract security concerns. They are part of Iran's recent experience.
European governments cannot reasonably expect Tehran to disregard these realities while simultaneously embracing the argument that their own deteriorating security environment justifies greater reliance on nuclear weapons.
Security cannot be treated as an exclusive privilege reserved for powerful countries. Nor can the principle of deterrence be considered legitimate for one group of nations and inherently unacceptable for another.
Why is Iran expected to accept a different set of rules?
Perhaps the most important question raised by Europe's nuclear shift concerns the future of the international non-proliferation regime itself.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) establishes obligations concerning the prevention of nuclear weapons proliferation, the peaceful use of nuclear energy and progress towards nuclear disarmament. Iran, as a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the treaty, has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes and that it is entitled to develop nuclear technology under the treaty's provisions.
The European powers, meanwhile, have increasingly embraced nuclear deterrence as an indispensable instrument of their own security. France and the United Kingdom already possess nuclear arsenals, while several other European NATO members participate in nuclear-sharing arrangements involving American weapons.
The problem is not simply that Europe possesses nuclear weapons or participates in deterrence arrangements. It is that European governments continue to approach the nuclear question through a framework that appears to grant themselves considerable strategic flexibility while demanding increasingly restrictive commitments from Iran.
The disparity becomes even more difficult to justify when the respective security environments are considered.
Iran faces threats from countries that possess overwhelming conventional military capabilities and, in the case of Israeli regime, an undeclared nuclear arsenal. It has also experienced direct military aggression from the United States and Israel. Meanwhile, European countries are increasingly citing the possibility of a confrontation with Russia as justification for strengthening their nuclear deterrence.
If the prospect of a potential conflict is sufficient to justify expanding Europe's nuclear capabilities, how can Iran's much more immediate and tangible security concerns be dismissed?
And if nuclear weapons are being presented as the ultimate guarantee of sovereignty and national survival, what alternative security guarantees are actually being offered to countries such as Iran?
A dangerous lesson for the international order
Europe's evolving nuclear posture sends a deeply troubling message to the rest of the world: international rules and non-proliferation commitments can be interpreted flexibly when the security interests of powerful countries are at stake.
This approach risks undermining the very international framework that European governments have repeatedly invoked in their dealings with Iran. It also raises serious questions about the credibility of European diplomacy and its ability to act as an impartial participant in negotiations over nuclear issues.
Ultimately, the issue is not whether Iran should acquire nuclear weapons. The right to peaceful nuclear technology, the question of nuclear weapons acquisition, and the broader right of every nation to defend its sovereignty are separate matters that should not be deliberately conflated.
The real question is why Europe believes it can determine the security requirements of other nations while reserving for itself the freedom to pursue whatever military capabilities it considers necessary.
If nuclear deterrence is a legitimate response to insecurity, then European governments must explain why Iran's security concerns deserve less consideration than their own. If nuclear militarisation is dangerous and destabilising, they must apply that principle consistently, rather than using it selectively as a political instrument against countries they regard as adversaries.
Europe cannot spend decades demanding that Iran demonstrate restraint while simultaneously preparing for a nuclear confrontation of its own.
The world cannot be expected to accept a system in which the powerful are entitled to pursue nuclear deterrence, while the less powerful are told that their security must depend on the goodwill of those same powers.

articles.title: North Korea tests cluster-bomb warhead for ballistic missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea tested a “Standard Type 2” cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31, claiming it can destroy 12 to 13 hectares.
- The Missile Administration said units will be able to use four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year.
North Korea tested a cluster-bomb warhead for its tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31 and said it will let its military units choose from four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year, state news agency KCNA reported on Nov. 1.
The Missile Administration, which runs North Korea’s missile development, said the test assessed the warhead’s combat readiness and destructive power. Its Ballistic Missile System Institute and Warhead Institute said they confirmed that the “Standard Type 2” cluster warhead can destroy a target area of 12 to 13 hectares, about 30 to 32 acres. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Military Commission and first vice director of a Central Committee department, oversaw the test. Leader Kim Jong Un was not reported to have attended.
KCNA did not name the missile or give its range, altitude or launch site. The missile was fired at an uninhabited island target in the West Sea, also known as the Yellow Sea, South Korea’s JKN reported, and analysts said it appears to be the first time North Korea has fired a cluster-armed missile from a wheeled mobile launcher.
“We classify the cluster-bomb warheads into four categories according to special and standard purposes. Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the DPRK Missile Administration.
A cluster warhead opens in the air and scatters dozens or hundreds of small bomblets over a wide area, making it effective against troops, vehicles, artillery positions and airfields rather than a single hardened target. Neither North Korea nor South Korea has joined the international convention banning cluster munitions.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launch on the day it happened, a break from its usual practice of reporting North Korean ballistic missile launches in real time. The military said on Nov. 1 that it had tracked related activity before the launch in close information sharing with the United States and maintained a readiness posture. Because the missile flew a short range at low altitude, the military wanted to complete its analysis before confirming it was a ballistic missile, Financial News reported.
North Korea has tested cluster warheads on its tactical missiles before. In April, it tested a Hwasong-11A short-range ballistic missile with a cluster warhead alongside other new weapons, and later that month Kim Jong Un watched the launch of Hwasong-11 Ra missiles fitted with cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads, which state media also claimed could devastate an area of about 13 hectares.
The test came two days after North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area during a firepower demonstration tied to a drone exhibition, where Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The Missile Administration described the Oct. 31 launch as part of regular research work to improve the power of its weapon systems.

articles.title: Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
articles.body:
Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday morning, checking in amid preparations for possible strikes on Iran, the Wall Street Journal has reported, citing people familiar with the call.
According to the WSJ, Trump had earlier held another meeting with senior military commanders at the White House to discuss options for resuming major combat operations. Over the past few weeks, multiple media outlets have reported that the US could resume strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb Iran, warning of “another little Epic Fury” if Tehran fails to meet his peace terms. US officials have reportedly warned Arab allies hosting American military bases to prepare for a short but intense operation.
Asked at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida on Saturday night whether he expected to “go back to war with Iran” in the coming weeks, Trump replied: “Let’s say I did – would I tell you? I can’t tell you this.”
The Pentagon has reportedly presented Trump with potential targets ranging from Iranian nuclear facilities and underground military sites to Kharg Island, a major oil export hub in the Persian Gulf. The US has also been sending additional missile interceptors to the region and relocating troops from vulnerable bases.
According to a Jerusalem Post report published on Saturday, the US and Israel have already drawn up plans for renewed military action, but Trump is unlikely to order strikes before Tuesday’s vote unless intelligence indicates preparations for a surprise attack.
A resumption of hostilities would come at a sensitive time for Netanyahu, whose right-wing bloc failed to secure a parliamentary majority in last week’s election. He will remain in office as coalition negotiations continue.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump had not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran but preferred a diplomatic solution. His remarks came as Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha following more than 12 hours of discussions in Tehran on Friday. A source familiar with the talks told Reuters that diplomacy was being coordinated through regular contacts with Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had reviewed a letter from US Vice President J.D. Vance aimed at reopening negotiations, describing the initiative as a “positive step.”
Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered the armed forces to prepare for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by his office on Saturday.

articles.title: Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
articles.body:
Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN - In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
*Mahdi Zolfaghari is an associate professor in the Department of Asian Studies at Allameh Tabataba’i University

articles.title: Greece receives second FDI frigate HS Nearchos
articles.body:
- Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, Greece’s second FDI frigate, at Lorient on Oct. 30, ten months after the first ship, HS Kimon.
- The third Greek frigate is due by the end of 2026, and a fourth, ordered in November 2025, is scheduled for 2028.
Naval Group handed over HS Nearchos, the second of Greece’s new French-built defense and intervention frigates, to the Hellenic Navy at its shipyard in Lorient, France, on Oct. 30, ten months after Greece received the first ship of the class.
Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin attended the ceremony. The third Greek frigate, HS Formion, is due by the end of 2026, which would give the Hellenic Navy three of the ships within a year, the company said. Naval Group did not say when Nearchos will sail for Greece or enter operational service.
“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honour to deliver the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, HS Nearchos, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin and Nikos Dendias, whom I would like to thank for their renewed trust,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The FDI, short for Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention, is a French design of about 4,500 tons and 122 m (400 feet) built for air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine warfare. Greece’s version, known as the FDI HN or Kimon class, carries a heavier weapons fit than the French Navy’s ships, with Thales Sea Fire radar and up to 32 Aster 30 long-range air defense missiles. Greece is also buying Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 drones to fly from Kimon, Nearchos and Formion for surveillance and anti-submarine work.
The first ship, HS Kimon, was delivered on Dec. 18, 2025, and arrived in Greece in January. In March, Greece sent it to Cyprus to help defend the island against Iranian attacks, alongside a Hydra-class frigate and F-16 fighters, its first operational mission. At the time, Kimon was the only Greek warship able to provide long-range air defense, Naval News reported.
Greece agreed in September 2021 to buy three of the frigates, with an option for a fourth, in a package worth about €3 billion including weapons, and the program started in 2022. It exercised the option in November 2025, ordering a fourth ship, HS Themistokles, along with maintenance and upgrades for the whole fleet. That ship is due in 2028.
More than 75 Greek companies are involved in Naval Group’s frigate and submarine programs for Greece, supplying parts ranging from electronic maps to pre-outfitted hull blocks and complex mechanical and electronic systems, the company said. Naval Group has committed to 25% local content on the fourth frigate. It has also won the initial in-service support contract for the Greek FDIs, which it will carry out with its Greek subsidiary, Naval Group Hellas, and local partners.
The Greek ships are part of a larger order book. Thirteen FDIs have now been ordered for three NATO navies, five for France, four for Greece and four for Sweden, and Naval Group says its Lorient yard can now deliver two of the frigates a year.

articles.title: Iran warns new war could last longer as Trump threatens strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes
Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to "take care" of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the US and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
In the most intense phase of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks across the region. Iran-aligned armed groups joined the fighting in Lebanon and Yemen.
Akraminia's remarks followed Trump's suggestion that the US could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.
"We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
US media reported that Trump held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday over whether and when to ramp up combat operations against Iran.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with the Islamic republic, with Netanyahu pressing the president to strike Iran immediately after the US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as "tough," while the US source said it was "direct," according to Axios.
'No geographical limitations'
Top military and political officials in Iran have warned against any new attack.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday echoed a warning issued a day earlier in a written message by Iran's new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
"In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy," Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said "we hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy", adding that Iran "remains prepared for both defence and diplomacy", according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in "tone" from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, "neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations".
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The US has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The US has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

'Braced for the worst'
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates hoped the exchanges would yield a breakthrough but was preparing for the worst.
"We're hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough," he told a conference in Manama.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round ... But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."

Others including 48-year-old vendor Ebrahim saw no reason to be concerned.

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine will stop hitting Russia’s refineries if US provides missiles
articles.body:
Zelensky says Ukraine will stop hitting Russia’s refineries if US provides missiles
WASHINGTON - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Nov 1 that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries – a key demand of US President Donald Trump – if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.
Trump, battling inflation at home driven in large part by soaring energy prices fuelled by his war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, has demanded the European foes stop attacking each other’s energy sites.
Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News on Nov 1, Zelensky said he had had “different and several” conversations with Trump and his team about the issue.
“We asked that we can’t not respond after Russia’s attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything,” he told Fox News host Trey Yingst.
“We said that if you want us not to attack Russia’s refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid.”
Zelensky said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month, Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period.
Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles.
Asked if he was concerned that this would be seen as trying to “leverage” Trump, Zelensky answered in the negative.
“I don’t have any concerns when I share the truth between partners,” he said.
The Trump administration on Oct 30 green-lit the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the State Department said, but the Ukrainian president warned deliveries could take years.
Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.
Last week, Zelensky suggested that US and European allies could give his country missiles from their stockpiles, which would later be replenished by the new purchase authorized on Oct 30.
The longest truce of the Ukraine war, limited to the eastern Kherson region, ended on Nov 1 after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February. AFP

articles.title: Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
articles.body:
Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
- North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers are blamed for a record US$6 billion Binance crypto theft. US authorities say the group is linked to Lazarus and Pyongyang’s cyber warfare programme.
- TraderTraitor uses fake job offers and malware to steal data and digital assets. The FBI says hackers have also hit DMM Bitcoin, Atomic Wallet, Alphapo, CoinsPaid and Bybit.
- Stolen crypto is laundered through mixing services and private exchanges, then used for weapons research and procurement. Analysts say cybercrime gives North Korea fast money despite sanctions.
AI generated
SEOUL – North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by the US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (S$7.7 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.
The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberthefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyberwarfare programme:
Who are they?
TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cybercapabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyberforce, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.
“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.
In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?
High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, the US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing some US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.
The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, AlphaPo and Coinspaid.
The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?
The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyberactivity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.
“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cybertheft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim.
“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. 
AFP

articles.title: Iran’s army warns that any new war with US could be ‘longer than previous conflict’

Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes

Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the US and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
“A potential future war could last longer than (the) previous conflict, and the American President would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
He was referring to the most intense phase of the fighting in the war that began on Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, killing the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state TV.

“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters at his Florida residence.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said “we hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy”, adding that Iran “remains prepared for both defence and diplomacy”, according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Oct 31 that he had received a letter from US Vice-President J.D. Vance seeking to revive talks.
He noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, “neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations”.
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The US has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
‘Braced for the worst’
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Nov 1 that the United Arab Emirates hoped that the exchanges would yield a breakthrough but was preparing for the worst.
“We’re hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough,” he told a conference in Manama, Bahrain.
“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst.”
In Tehran, some residents described a sense of helplessness as threats of renewed fighting mount.
“The news coming in is truly worrying. However, no matter how much I, as an ordinary citizen, immerse myself in these reports, there is nothing I can actually do about it,” Mohadese, a 27-year-old health inspector, told AFP.

articles.title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
articles.body:
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
- Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in four regions, while Ukraine said it hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, linked to missile production.
- Nizhny Novgorod governor Gleb Nikitin said a Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial site, and fuel officials warned against “panic buying”.
- Both sides kept up long-range attacks despite a local ceasefire near Oleshky. Russia said it downed 235 drones, while Ukraine said it shot down 371 of 433 Russian drones.
AI generated
KYIV – Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Nov 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while the Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no let-up in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelensky said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since the evening of Oct 31.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as at the morning of Nov 1. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
Fuel supplies
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying”, Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Oct 30, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Nov 1, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices. REUTERS

articles.title: After fake alerts in Ukraine, someone hacked Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry app and announced the threat of a nuclear strike against the Russian Federation – ATESH
articles.body:
After fake alerts in Ukraine, someone hacked Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry app and announced the threat of a nuclear strike against the Russian Federation – ATESH
Kyiv • UNN
ATESH said that pro-Ukrainian hackers had hacked Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry app and sent out fake messages about a nuclear threat. There is no independent confirmation of the attack.
Pro-Ukrainian hackers allegedly hacked the Russian Emergencies Ministry’s app for emergency alerts and began sending messages about a fabricated nuclear threat. This happened overnight on November 2, following the alleged interference by Russian hackers in the operation of the Ukrainian "Air Raid Alert" app. The partisan movement ATESH reported the hacking of the Russian service, UNN writes.
Details
A published screenshot shows a message for residents of Voronezh Oblast, dated November 2 at 02:47. It allegedly announces the launch of nuclear warheads at all regions of Russia.
The authors of the alert urged Russians to stock up on food for three weeks and hide in basements. The message contained obscene language and was clearly provocative.
Russian media and local authorities in the regions later confirmed that the Emergencies Ministry’s services had been hacked.
The enemy hacked the official "Russian Emergencies Ministry" app and all the ministry’s regional channels on the MAX messenger! Several hours earlier, our hackers had hacked the Ukrainian alert app "Alert"
What preceded the alleged hack
On the evening of November 1, users of the Ukrainian "Air Raid Alert" app began receiving false notifications about nuclear, radiation and chemical threats, as well as the danger of street fighting.
Ukrainian officials warned that these messages were untrue. Unauthorized interference with the service was considered one of the possible causes of the incident.
In particular, the Kyiv City State Administration assured that there was no radiation threat to the capital, and that the "Kyiv Digital" app and the city’s alert system were operating normally.
Against this backdrop, ATESH claimed to have hacked the Russian Emergencies Ministry app. At the same time, there is currently no independent confirmation of the scale of the cyberattack or the number of users who received the fake messages.

articles.title: North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
articles.body:
North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

articles.title: Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends
articles.body:
Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends
Moscow and Kyiv continue strikes elsewhere, but no reported violations in Kherson region during the six-day ceasefire.
The longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine, limited to Ukraine’s eastern Kherson region, has come to an end with no violations reported by either side, but also no sign of an extension.
The truce, which ended on Sunday night, allowed hundreds of besieged residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation between Kyiv and Moscow.
Russian strikes elsewhere in Ukraine on Sunday left hundreds of thousands of households without power, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. In Russia, meanwhile, authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The six-day localised ceasefire in the front-line Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by United States First Lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo XIV. It was set to expire at 10:59pm Ukraine time (20:59 GMT).
On Sunday, Ukraine’s military said it evacuated 167 more people from threatened areas of the southern Kherson region, including 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
“Units of civil-military cooperation of the ‘South’ group of forces, in cooperation with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region,” Ukraine’s General Staff wrote on Telegram.
An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice to evacuate to Kyiv-controlled territory of Ukraine or territory occupied by Russia, or to remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
“The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack,” Melania Trump said on social media. “Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Moscow had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries’ human rights commissioners.
A Ukrainian official, however, told the AFP news agency that Russia reportedly refused an offer to extend the ceasefire after Kyiv’s Foreign Ministry proposed it.
Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022, Moscow’s forces have occupied most of the eastern Ukrainian regions of Donetsk and Luhansk, as well as the majority of territory in Ukraine’s southern Kherson and Zaporizhia regions.
Residents urged to remain vigilant
Kherson Governor Oleksandr Prokudin urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared on Sunday.
“I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called ‘red zones’ – areas and settlements near the Dnipro [River],” Prokudin wrote on Telegram. “The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high.”
Residents in Kherson city, one of the remaining areas of the region still controlled by Ukraine, remained calm, despite knowing the quiet of the localised ceasefire would soon end.
“Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert.
Knyha is from Oleshky and used to commute from there to Kherson for work. He has not given up hope of returning home.
“That’s also what keeps me here,” he told the Associated Press news agency.
Fighting elsewhere
Elsewhere, Moscow and Kyiv have continued air strikes, with Zelenskyy saying on Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter. Attacks on power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight cut electricity to hundreds of thousands of households, he said.
A Russian attack also killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia, when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded.
Russian drone attacks targeting Ukraine’s Kyiv region for a second consecutive day wounded a woman and damaged homes, energy infrastructure and a retail establishment, regional authorities said.
In its daily report on Sunday, Ukraine’s Air Force said that Moscow’s forces attacked Ukraine with 433 drones overnight, of which 371 were destroyed or suppressed.
Meanwhile, more than 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the skies of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow, Governor Gleb Nikitin said on Sunday.
The attack sparked a blaze at the Kstovo oil refinery, Russian media outlets reported, sharing images of black plumes of smoke over the horizon.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv also struck a factory for missile components and air defence facilities in Russia’s southern Rostov region.
“We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capability to continue it,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Houthis report airstrikes on Red Sea oil port, telecom facility in Yemen
articles.body:
SANAA/RIYADH, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Sunday evening that a series of airstrikes hit Ras Isa port, a key oil terminal on the Red Sea coast in the western province of Hodeidah, including a port berth and a commercial vessel docked there.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV attributed the strikes on Ras Isa port to what the group described as "Saudi aggression." The channel gave no immediate information on casualties or the extent of damage to the port or vessel.
The channel later reported another airstrike on a telecommunications facility southeast of Saada city, the capital of the Houthis' northern stronghold of Saada province, and attributed the attack to Saudi warplanes. No casualties were immediately reported.
Separately, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X on Sunday that 75 air and missile strikes had hit the provinces of Saada, Taiz, Amran, Ibb, Dhamar, Lahj, Hodeidah and Al-Jawf over the past 24 hours.
He claimed the attacks caused civilian casualties and brought the total number of air and missile strikes since the latest escalation began to 3,830. The figures could not be independently verified.
Also on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition announced that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone and a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's southern region.
Recent weeks have seen escalating cross-border hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with Saudi strikes hitting Houthi-held areas in Yemen and the Houthis launching missiles and drones toward Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■
