articles.title: NATO turns 5G towers into sensors in Baltic battlefield experiment
articles.body:
- NATO linked a Maven system to a national system in hours using agentic AI and ran a Lithuania-to-Latvia counter-drone engagement during DiBaX 2026.
- The Oct. 19-30 experiment in Latvia also tested military use of commercial 5G networks, jam-resistant communications and 5G-based object detection.
NATO linked a Maven targeting system to a national military system in a matter of hours using agentic artificial intelligence and ran a cross-border counter-drone engagement during a two-week experiment in Latvia, the alliance’s top transformation commander said on Oct. 30.
Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, described the results at Ādaži Military Base near Riga at the close of the Digital Backbone Experimentation, known as DiBaX 2026, which ran from Oct. 19 to 30. He said some tests failed along the way and that the alliance had deliberately accepted that risk.
“We have connected systems that were never designed to communicate with each other, using artificial intelligence to overcome interoperability barriers. It’s the first time that we have, for example, a Maven system that is speaking to a national system, and that has been fixed in hours with Agentic AI,” said Vandier.
NATO bought its own version of Palantir’s AI-enabled Maven Smart System in 2025 to help commanders pull together intelligence and speed up decisions, and has been rolling it out across its headquarters. Vandier did not say which country’s system Maven was connected to. Agentic AI refers to software that can carry out multistep tasks on its own, in this case working out how two systems exchange data.
The counter-drone test crossed a national border. A drone took off in Lithuania, flew into Latvia and was engaged there by a counter-drone system, Vandier said. It was one of several trials under NATO’s Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, which looks at how sensors and weapons from different countries and companies can work together as one layered defense against drones.
“Even if it didn’t work this morning, it has been done this week. So we had a drone taking off from Lithuania, arriving here and being engaged by a counter system,” said Vandier.
DiBaX itself tested three ways to keep NATO forces connected. In the first, organizers set up a private slice of a host country’s commercial 5G network, reserved and secured for military use, so arriving NATO forces could have command and data links from their first day before their own infrastructure arrived. The second tested automatic switching between communication paths when one is jammed, including radio across different frequencies, satellite links such as 5G direct-to-device, and troposcatter, which bounces radio signals off the lower atmosphere to reach beyond the horizon. The third used ordinary 5G cell towers as passive sensors to detect objects moving through their coverage, particularly in cities with dense tower networks. Vandier said a team of medics in the field also sent patient biodata over the network to doctors in the United States.
The scenarios were built around grey-zone incidents below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, such as drone incursions and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. A third track, Next Generation Targeting, tested AI-enabled decision support to shorten the time between collecting information and acting on it, and Vandier said the targeting process ran noticeably faster by the end of the week than at the start.
“For us, as a NATO member of the Alliance Eastern Flank here in Latvia, we cannot afford to treat technological innovation and adaptation as a distant objective for us,” said Lt. Gen. Kaspars Pudāns, commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces.
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, the United States, Canada, Finland and other allies took part, along with NATO bodies including the DIANA innovation accelerator and the NATO Communications and Information Agency. More than 60 technology companies joined, among them Ericsson, Nokia, Thales and Portuguese drone maker TEKEVER, with Latvian telecom company LMT acting as technical integrator. This was the fifth year in a row the experiment has been held in Latvia.
The event closed with NATO FUSE on Oct. 29 and 30, which included live field demonstrations. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, visited Latvia on Oct. 30 and met President Edgars Rinkēvičs. European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis used the event to announce two pilot European Drone Technology Hubs, one in Latvia and one in the Netherlands, to open in 2027 and speed up development and testing of drone and counter-drone technology in cooperation with NATO.
“The next challenge, and it’s the most difficult, is adoption,” said Vandier.

articles.title: Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
articles.body:
Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has accused his political opponents of receiving support from an “army of Russian bots”amid an escalating constitutional crisis in Warsaw. The pro-EU leader offered no proof for his claim, which came after a government-backed judge moved to oust two key officials supported by his rival, right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, from the Constitutional Tribunal, triggering public outrage.
Unrest erupted on Friday when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s governing majority, ordered the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. The tribunal’s existing leadership rejected the suspensions, declaring that all those participating in the attempted takeover “are committing the crime of a coup d’état.”
The development triggered street protests around the court building and a heavy police deployment. Nawrocki, who canceled a planned trip to Senegal, personally pushed his way into the tribunal to confront Korwin-Piotrowska and her allies, telling them that “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk scrambled to defend his actions, accusing his rivals of “seeking to destroy democracy and the rule of law.” The Polish PM, a strong supporter of EU integration who served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, has long criticized PiS judicial reforms – which he said undermined judges’ independence – as well as Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
“Is it greed, stupidity or treason?” Tusk asked, claiming that the opposition was receiving support from “pro-Russian forces worldwide.”
“In this conflict, they’re using an army of Russian bots online. In fact, they’ve even received public compliments from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue,” the prime minister claimed, without providing further proof or elaborating.
Moscow has repeatedly said it does not interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs. While Russian officials have yet to respond to Tusk’s allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in July denied that Russia was responsible for cyberattacks on Polish energy infrastructure.
Responding to Tusk’s address, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, called the prime minister a “pathological liar” and accused him of setting Poland ablaze while pretending to extinguish the fire. “It’s hard to find a single word, expression, or sentence that would be true, that would reflect the actual or legal reality,” he added.
Tusk’s accusation comes after several Western media outlets, anti-Russia hawks, and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky propagated the claim that Kiev’s drone strikes, which damaged several data centers operated by Russian technology giant Yandex, crippled alleged Russian bot networks supporting Western right-wing movements, including Germany’s AfD and US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.
However, several independent investigations by cybersecurity and research firms quickly debunked the narrative. Experts in particular pointed out that one viral graph supposedly showing a collapse in AfD-related activity was found to contain fabricated or unverifiable figures.
Commenting on the chaos, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described it as a “constitutional coup.” He suggested that “Brussels’ protégé Tusk” was persecuting PiS conservatives over the latter’s hostility toward Ukrainian Nazi collaborators. Medvedev concluded by sarcastically invoking an old schoolyard joke, saying, “And these are the people who scold my brother and me for picking our noses.”

articles.title: Attack boats stayed in harbour all summer, report warns
articles.body:
Britain’s attack submarine fleet spent the summer tied up in harbour while Russian activity around British waters increased, and the availability of escorts for the ballistic missile boats that carry the nuclear deterrent is among the consequences raised, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The paper, the first in a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy, opens by saying: “The Royal Navy is gripped by a critical but needless decline in strategic capacity, as demonstrated by a steep reduction in both mass and readiness.
“This comes at a time of intensifying maritime competition and growing threats to British national interests. These threats are most acute in and around British waters, as Russia’s submarines, warships and even its shadow-fleet carrying illicit Russian oil across the globe, are all increasing their operations off Britain’s coasts.”
It records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, that operations to track Russian activity rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year, and that Russian warships made repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and the North Sea. Ministers have confirmed that Moscow uses commercial proxies to threaten undersea infrastructure, and the paper cites analysis uncovering five hundred incidents of Russian civilian vessels loitering above cables.
Concerns about the frigate and destroyer fleets are set out alongside the navy’s transition to automation through the hybrid navy concept, before the paper turns to its main subject. It says: “However, it is in the submarine fleet that we see an especially stark vulnerability and where, due to its purposes, creates unique threats to Britain’s security.”
On the Astute class, which numbers five in service with two more being readied, the paper states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” That finding draws on reporting by Navy Lookout, and the Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
Turning to the four Vanguard boats, the paper acknowledges that deployment cycles are not discussed publicly and then sets out what it describes as widely understood. It says: “Due to the nature of their deterrent, HM Government rightly does not comment on their deployment cycles or current state. However, it is widely understood that the fleet has been in a poor state for some years.”
Designed for patrols of three to four months, the boats have run planned patrols of under a hundred days well past that mark. The paper says: “Most SSN- and SSBN-operating navies view 100-day patrols as the sensible maximum; at least the last ten deterrent patrols all exceeded five months in duration, up until April this year, with the last coming in at over 200 days, apparently becoming the new normal.”
On the four Dreadnought boats due in the early 2030s, the paper argues that work on their successor cannot wait, since each is designed for thirty years of service and the build alone takes twenty. The Ministry of Defence accepted the Strategic Defence Review’s recommendation to begin early definition and requirement-setting during this parliamentary term, a pledge affirmed in July, and the paper says: “However, this pledge was only affirmed in July 2026, and there have been no major announcements since; with only two full Parliamentary years left before the next General Election must be called, the Government needs to properly commit to Dreadnought’s successor at the earliest opportunity.”
The sharpest warnings concern SSN-AUKUS, where steel cutting on the first British boat is scheduled at Barrow-in-Furness in 2027. The paper says: “Given the likely concurrent Astute and Dreadnought programmes, the sole UK submarine construction site in Barrow-in-Furness risks facing acute labour shortfalls as soon as SSN-AUKUS begins. In the meantime the site has added only about 500 workers against a required 2,500 to run the parallel Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS build lines.
“The projected build-timeframes for SSN-AUKUS are also deeply concerning. Astute-class boats averaged 128 months to build; SSN-AUKUS are projected to take only 18 months each. This feels unrealistic, and risks cost overruns, delays, supply-chain over-stretch, and potentially an even bigger ‘submarine gap’.”
Describing the programme as Pillar One of AUKUS and saying it must not fail, the paper adds: “However, without guarantees of resource from HM Government that are currently absent, and instead a vague pledge of total vessels built, a lack of political leadership and gaps in the defence-industrial base, Britain risks being the weak link in the partnership.”
Four recommendations follow, covering a firm commitment to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats at the spring Spending Review in 2027, increased resources for the Astute class to clear maintenance backlogs and dockyard constraints, a standing requirement for two of the five Astutes to be deployable and operational at all times, and the commissioning of the Dreadnought successor definition phase by the close of 2027.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time, covering land, space and naval capability with a foreword by General the Lord Dannatt. The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain has allowed its under-ice submarine capability to lapse and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters, and the Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

articles.title: Riots and clashes with police marked youth protests in Germany
articles.body:
Youth protests in more than 30 German cities against the possible introduction of compulsory military service and in support of better education and social justice have escalated into clashes with police and riots. Several police officers were injured, and in Frankfurt demonstrators smashed shop windows, ransacked shops and stole goods. This is reported by DPA.
The protests were organized at the call of the youth movement "Generation Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt). According to organizers, more than 100,000 people took part in the demonstrations across the country. Participants expressed dissatisfaction not only with the possible return of compulsory military service, but also with insufficient funding for education, the rising cost of living, the lack of sufficient measures against climate change and social inequality.
Although most demonstrations were peaceful, tensions escalated in several major cities and clashes with law enforcement.
The most serious unrest was recorded in Frankfurt, where the protest began peacefully in the early afternoon along the Main River. Police said up to 8,000 people took part in the march, while organizers said around 9,000.
However, in the evening, the situation in the city center became more tense. Some of the demonstrators began throwing stones, bottles and firecrackers at the police, which forced the police to end the demonstration. The police used water cannons and pepper spray to disperse the crowd. Several police officers were injured, one of whom may have suffered more serious injuries, said Roman Pozek, the interior minister of the state of Hesse. According to him, about 100 representatives of left-wing extremist circles took part in the attacks on the police.
BTA/AP
The violence continued after the demonstration was dispersed. Groups of rioters smashed the windows of several commercial establishments and looted shops in the city center. Sports shoes and other goods were stolen, and among the attacked establishments was a specialized firearms store. According to police, Molotov cocktails were even thrown at law enforcement officers and emergency services teams.
The situation around Zeil, one of the main shopping streets in Frankfurt, was particularly tense, with a significant police contingent stationed there.
There were also riots in Hamburg. Several thousand people joined the protest march there, and some of the participants, dressed in black and some with masks on their faces, tore down plastic barriers from a road repair area and set them on fire near a subway station. Police intervened with pepper spray, and the fire was extinguished with a water cannon. According to organizers, between 6,000 and 7,000 people participated in the demonstration.
In Berlin, fireworks were also used during a protest in the central Mitte district. About 700 people gathered at Rosenthaler Platz, from where they headed to the Prenzlauer Berg district. Police warned demonstrators not to use fireworks and to refrain from violence. According to law enforcement, representatives of left-wing political circles and pro-Palestinian movements were among the participants.
Due to the previously announced demonstrations, German authorities had taken enhanced security measures. Additional police forces, water cannons and drones were deployed in a number of cities.
BTA/AP
The protests showed that discontent among some young Germans spans a wide range of issues, from the prospect of compulsory military service to education, social policy and the cost of living. Despite the largely peaceful nature of the demonstrations, clashes and subsequent vandalism in Frankfurt and other cities marked the day of protests.

articles.title: Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
articles.body:
Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on U.S. military bases across the Middle East, according to a sweeping Wall Street Journal investigation that offers the fullest public picture yet of what the war on Iran has cost American forces in the region.
The Journal's analysis, drawing on satellite imagery, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials, identified 274 damaged structures at 24 installations with an American military presence during the war's first six months.
The investigation found that Iran increasingly targeted buildings where American troops live and sleep, showing an improved ability to sequence attacks and strike with greater precision.
While the Pentagon has priced the damage to bases at a minimum of $5 billion, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter cited by The Journal, a separate person briefed on the cost said the figure could reach as high as $15 billion.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which reviewed the Journal's findings on damaged buildings, estimated that reconstruction alone would top $4 billion, a figure that excludes replacing the equipment and systems housed inside.
Those repairs come on top of the war's overall cost, which stood at $47.1 billion as of Oct. 16, according to a document viewed by The Journal.
According to an Associated Press analysis, Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The Journal also said the human toll has also mounted. More than 20 U.S. service members have died in activity related to the war since it began on Feb. 28, according to Defense Department data, and more than 400 were wounded before a temporary ceasefire collapsed in July. After that, the government stopped publishing casualty figures specific to the conflict.

articles.title: Ukraine says public air raid alert app sent false alerts after being hacked
articles.body:
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Ukraine’s Air Force said on Sunday that the public air raid alert app had been hacked.
The app for a short time showed Kyiv and other areas subject to nuclear and chemical alerts and the threat of street combat. An erroneous message said Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force said on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!”
The abnormality later disappeared.
Ukraine’s Ministry for Digital Transformation said the app was not in operation, but other means of alerting the public were functioning as were air raid sirens.
In a separate event, the mobile app of Russia’s emergencies ministry was hit by a massive cyberattack that resulted in the spread of false information to the public, state news agency TASS quoted the ministry as saying early on Monday.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.
(Reporting by Ron Popeski, Bogdan Kochubey and Jekaterīna Golubkova; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Stephen Coates)

articles.body:
MOSCOW, November 1. /TASS/. Denmark is deeply involved in the Ukrainian conflict and currently serves as a logistical base for the Ukrainian armed forces, Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin said in an interview with TASS.

articles.title: Trump holds call with Netanyahu over state of Iran war: Report
articles.body:
Trump holds call with Netanyahu over state of Iran war: Report
- Trump spoke with Netanyahu about Iran war strikes and talks. Netanyahu wanted immediate attacks, while Trump said negotiations were "going fine" and he was not rushing.
- Axios said the call was "tough" and "direct". Trump is using both air strikes and diplomacy, while seeking a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
- The call came as Iran and mediators showed signs of renewed talks. Trump also faces political pressure at home over gas prices and rising living costs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump held a call with Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu over when and whether to ramp up combat operations against Iran, US media reported on Nov 1.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders on Oct 31 discussed the state of negotiations with the Islamic republic, with Netanyahu pressing the president to launch strikes on Iran immediately after the US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as “tough”, while the American source said it was “direct,” according to Axios.
Throughout the eight-month war, Trump has pursued dual tracks with Tehran: a campaign of air strikes and other attacks, while seeking to reach a deal that would jumpstart peace talks and fully open the Strait of Hormuz to vital oil and gas traffic.
On Oct 31, the president maintained to reporters that negotiations with Iran to end the war were “going fine”, and that there were still one or two targets to “take care” of.
He stressed too that Washington was not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran’s military and its nuclear program.
The Trump-Netanyahu talks followed the disclosure on Oct 31 by Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei that he had received a letter from US Vice-President JD Vance seeking to revive stalled talks.
In another sign that mediators are keen to resume negotiations, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Oct 30 for talks with Iranian officials, state media reported.
Trump has faced immense political pressure over the Middle East war, with US midterm voters furious over rising gas prices and other cost-of-living hikes – and they could potentially vent that anger at the ballot box. AFP

articles.title: Ukraine flies the first drone rescues of wounded troops
articles.body:
Ukraine has carried out the world’s first medical evacuations by heavy uncrewed aircraft, lifting wounded soldiers out of positions that could not be reached from the ground, and is developing evacuation drones as a dedicated capability of its own, according to the Ukrainian defence ministry.
Brave1, the defence innovation cluster working with the Ministry of Defence, set the requirement in 2024 after working with the military to define what such an aircraft would have to do. The criteria given to the defence technology market were that the aircraft must reliably carry 130 kilograms over a distance of at least fifteen kilometres and must carry an integrated communication system with at least three alternative types to survive in an electronic warfare environment, with lidar, optical stabilisation and navigation that works without satellites listed as options.
The first of those evacuations took place in October, when an infantryman of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was lifted out of a position the enemy had blocked. A Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 hexacopter built by a Brave1 participant flew the mission, an aircraft weighing 98 kilograms with a payload capacity of 130 kilograms, and it covered more than fifteen kilometres on the outbound leg.
Preparation ran to months and drew on the experience of the uncrewed ground vehicle company of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade. Equipment had been dropped to the soldier in advance and he had to secure himself to the aircraft’s winch without help, while adjacent units launched bomber drones to pull enemy interceptors away from the rescue aircraft.
A second system, Stargate, was built specifically for evacuation at the request of assault troops. It deploys in ten minutes, carries 150 kilograms at speeds up to 105 kilometres an hour and holds a medical module with a stretcher, and its software can plot a route and return to a safe area without help if navigation is completely jammed.
Assault troops of the CODE 9.2 regiment used it twice in a single week to bring out severely wounded soldiers from the grey zone five kilometres from the Russian border, where terrain, water obstacles and first person view drones ruled out any ground rescue. The aircraft flew nearly thirty kilometres each way and came back with the casualties aboard while under electronic attack, relying on artificial intelligence alone for navigation, with heavy strike drones suppressing enemy positions to cover the run.
Conventional casualty evacuation has become close to impossible along much of the front because the density of drone coverage turns any vehicle movement into a target, and uncrewed ground vehicles took over much of the work at the cost of speed. Survival after serious trauma depends heavily on reaching surgical care quickly, and a crawling robot moving along a mined route can take many hours to cover ground a helicopter would cross in minutes.
Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency has contracted three times as many uncrewed systems of all types this year as it did last year.

articles.title: America is using negotiations to buy time
articles.body:
America is using negotiations to buy time
Strategic affairs analyst Saeed Leilaz examined the letter sent by J.D. Vance to Mohsen Rezaei in an interview with the Etemad newspaper. The timing of the letter is significant because it comes amid heightened political and economic uncertainty. Leilaz argues that although the letter has been presented as an attempt to revive negotiations, it is accompanied by warnings and threats against Iranian infrastructure.
After failing to achieve certain military objectives, Washington has shifted toward a strategy designed to gain time, reduce attention on Iran's leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, and prepare the ground for stronger future pressure if necessary. Iran should respond through a balanced strategy that combines deterrence and diplomacy. He emphasizes the importance of maintaining military readiness, strengthening economic resilience, removing domestic obstacles to economic growth, and supporting productive sectors of the economy. Diplomatic channels should remain open, and negotiations should continue in a careful and calculated manner.
Kayhan: Trump seeks to portray himself as a victim
In an article, Kayhan argued that the conflict involving Iran has generated significant difficulties for both the United States and Europe. Many observers view the consequences of the confrontation as costly and destabilizing. Political pressure has become particularly intense for Trump. Developments linked to the conflict, combined with domestic challenges and election-related concerns, have forced him to modify his public messaging. Whereas he previously suggested that the conflict would have only a limited impact on the United States, he is now placing greater emphasis on portraying America as a target rather than an initiator. The newspaper also highlights rising energy concerns and continuing volatility in global oil prices. According to its analysis, expectations that economic conditions would rapidly improve have not been fulfilled. As a result, Trump is attempting to shift responsibility for the crisis onto Iran while presenting himself as responding to Iranian actions. This change in rhetoric is a sign of political weakness.
Iran: Diplomacy remains the best path for crisis management
The Iran newspaper focused on Tehran's proposed seven-day initiative, which was reportedly delivered through intermediaries. The analysis presents the proposal as a possible framework for reducing tensions and creating conditions for renewed diplomacy. The initiative is based on a series of reciprocal and phased measures. It seeks to connect several objectives, including ending hostilities, easing restrictions, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and creating a pathway toward renewed nuclear negotiations. Supporters believe that linking these elements together could establish clearer expectations for both sides and reduce uncertainty. The newspaper argues that the proposal may help build trust by providing a structured roadmap rather than relying on general political commitments. It further suggests that the framework could serve as a starting point for broader crisis management and help prevent the continuation of a cycle of escalation and retaliation. However, the paper stresses that implementation depends on political will and the readiness of all parties to take corresponding steps. Without reciprocal action, even a well-designed proposal is unlikely to succeed.
Khorasan: Decoding Vance's approach
Khorasan examined the possible objectives behind Vance's communication with Iran. According to the newspaper, American officials are eager to secure a diplomatic achievement before Nov. 3 midterm elections and view an agreement with Tehran as politically valuable. Washington reportedly wants nuclear issues to be incorporated into any broader arrangement. Tehran, however, is unwilling to accept such conditions under the current circumstances. Because the exact contents of the message remain unclear, Khorasan focuses on the broader political implications. The newspaper identifies two possible tactics. The first involves highlighting particular negotiating figures in an attempt to exploit perceived domestic divisions within Iran. The second involves introducing new conditions that could replace or alter previous understandings reached between the parties. Despite these concerns, Khorasan emphasizes that Iran remains willing to engage in dialogue. Nevertheless, it argues that successful negotiations require changes in Washington's approach and greater attention to Iranian concerns and conditions.
Hamshahri: Response without geographical limitations
Hamshahri discussed a Saturday order from the Leader of the Islamic Revolution to the armed forces in the event of resumption of war against Iran by pointing to the views of regional affairs analyst Seyyed Morteza Mousavi. According to Mousavi, the order emphasized preparedness, deterrence, and the ability to respond rapidly to any future threat. He identified three main themes: maintaining full readiness, delivering immediate and effective responses to threats, and ensuring that Iran would determine the course and duration of any future confrontation if attacked. Mousavi argued that recent conflicts demonstrated the importance of deterrence and military readiness in shaping regional security calculations. He also stated that any country allowing its territory or facilities to be used in attacks against Iran could face consequences in the event of future hostilities. In his interpretation, the order was intended to signal determination that responses to future threats would not necessarily be confined to a specific geographical area.

articles.title: Trump says US still has ‘one or two targets’ in Iran
articles.body:
Trump says US still has ‘one or two targets’ in Iran
- Trump said the US has destroyed much of Iran’s military and nuclear programme, but still has “one or two sites” to hit, including a suspected complex at Pickaxe Mountain.
- Iran warned of an “immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response” if attacked, while its leaders ordered new target lists and kept the Strait of Hormuz blockade in place.
- Diplomatic efforts continue through Qatar and Pakistan, but no deal has been reached. The conflict has lifted oil prices and could affect US and Israeli politics.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump said on Oct 31 that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
He said the US is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran’s military and nuclear programme.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters at his Florida residence.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.
Earlier on Oct 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran’s supreme leader on Oct 31 warned the US and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats that they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.
Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the US midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a “historic, one-time opportunity” to topple the Iranian government.
The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted in a general election on Oct 27 but yet to form a new government.
“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response,” Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders, according to a statement.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and the military’s top brass.
He has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in US-Israeli strikes.
Rubio warned that “we can achieve military objectives if we seek to”, adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.
Oil price spike
Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iran has previously warned that it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported on Oct 31.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 30 that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.
The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump’s ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu’s political camp with the most seats in Parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.
‘Flames of war’
Fresh diplomatic efforts are under way to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran on Oct 30, and US Vice-President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
“I read the letter,” said Rezaei, in a video broadcast on Iranian television. “I haven’t yet responded. Their tone has completely changed,” he added, describing that as “a good sign”, without going into more detail.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no plans for meetings with US officials.
“Iran’s conditions are clear and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
“The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” he said on social media.
Araghchi warned on X that there would no longer be any “red lines”. AFP

articles.title: What Ukraine can use to replace the scarce Patriot missiles as early as this winter: experts name possible options
articles.body:
What Ukraine can use to replace the scarce Patriot missiles as early as this winter: experts name possible options
Kyiv • UNN
The delivery of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles could take years due to the 24-month production timeline. For the winter, European stocks and Japan are being considered.
Ukraine may receive additional interceptor missiles for Patriot systems from European partners or Japan to strengthen protection against Russian ballistic missiles this winter. At the same time, it would be unwise to count on the rapid delivery of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, the sale of which has been approved by the United States. Defense Express reports this, according to UNN.
Details
The U.S. Department of State has approved the sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, along with spare parts and equipment, worth approximately $2.1 billion. The funding will be provided by Canada, Germany, and Norway במסגרת the JUMPSTART program, as well as through funds associated with an EU loan.
However, the main contractor for the deal is manufacturer Lockheed Martin, and the full production cycle for one missile takes approximately 24 months. Therefore, the delivery of all 500 interceptors could take several years, even if Ukraine's order is given priority.
Where Ukraine could obtain missiles this winter
According to Defense Express, one of the most realistic short-term options is the transfer of PAC-3 MSE missiles from the stocks of European allies, particularly Poland and Germany.
These countries have already transferred such interceptors to Ukraine. However, the number would likely be measured in dozens of missiles rather than hundreds. In addition, the partners need guarantees that their own stocks will be replenished quickly.
Another potential source is Japan—the only country that has localized PAC-3 MSE production. Japanese officials had previously indicated that the transfer of surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine was possible, but there have been no specific decisions regarding this particular modification yet.
Will new air defense systems help?
In the long term, French-Italian SAMP/T NG systems equipped with Ground Fire 300 radars could become an alternative to Patriot.
Ukraine expects to receive four such systems starting in 2027. Therefore, it is currently not possible to count on them as a solution for the winter of 2026–2027.
Another promising area is the European FREYJA antiballistic system project, whose first tests are scheduled for early 2027.
Defense Express emphasizes that even 500 new PAC-3 MSE missiles would not solve the shortage problem for long. With an estimated need of approximately 150 interceptors per month, such a stockpile would last only slightly more than three months.

articles.title: UK flies Protector drone on first home operation against Russian frigate
articles.body:
- An RAF Protector RG1 flew its first operational sorties in UK airspace, providing more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel.
- The aircraft supported HMS Dauntless and HMS Tyne as they tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14.
An RAF Protector RG1 remotely piloted aircraft has flown its first operational missions in UK airspace, giving the Royal Navy more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel while warships tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
The unarmed Protector flew alongside military and civilian air traffic while the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33) and offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) monitored Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships through the Channel between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14. The ministry did not say how many sorties the aircraft flew, which sensors it used or how much of the frigate’s transit it covered.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence. Working alongside Royal Navy vessels, it provided persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage, highlighting its ability to operate seamlessly across military and civilian airspace in support of maritime security, NATO commitments and wider UK tasking,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
Protector is the RAF’s version of General Atomics’ MQ-9B SkyGuardian, flown from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire by 31 and XIII squadrons. The UK Military Aviation Authority issued it a military type certificate on April 29, 2025, clearing it to fly without geographic restrictions in UK airspace, and it entered service in June 2025 as the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to do so. The MQ-9A Reaper it replaced never flew in UK airspace during its RAF career. The first of 16 Protectors arrived at RAF Waddington in 2023.
The RAF lists the aircraft’s endurance at more than 30 hours and its ceiling at up to 40,000 feet (12,200 m), with full-motion video, infrared imagery, synthetic aperture radar and ground target tracking among its sensors. In June 2026, a Protector flew from Waddington to RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus through European civil airspace, covering more than 2,000 nautical miles in about 13.5 hours.
The Channel mission was one of several Royal Navy operations against Russian ships between late September and mid-October. Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose deployed to Glasgow Prestwick Airport under Operation Iceblast, a test of how quickly the Merlin force can operate away from its home base. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 8, they tracked the Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship Viktor Leonov near the Outer Hebrides, where NATO’s Exercise Strike Warrior was underway with more than 2,000 personnel from six nations.
From Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, HMS Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron followed the Ropucha-class landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin, the cargo ship MV Energy-2 and the tug Proton through the Channel as they headed for the Baltic.
“HMS Dauntless monitored the movements of RFN Neustrashimy during her transit through the English Channel, contributing to the wider maritime picture and supporting UK maritime security,” said Commander Neil Skinner, commanding officer of HMS Dauntless.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements rose 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry said. Most of that work falls to patrol ships, frigates and helicopters; in January, HMS Mersey, HMS Severn and a Wildcat shadowed a Russian corvette and tanker through the same waters in a two-day operation coordinated with NATO allies.
“For the first time, Protector has joined Royal Navy warships and helicopters monitoring activity around our shores, demonstrating how we are constantly innovating to monitor and deter threats and irresponsible provocation,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The ministry tied the operations to £298 billion (about $399 billion) in planned defense spending over the next four years and a commitment to reach 3% of GDP on defense in 2030. It also pointed to £330 million (about $442 million) over four years to protect undersea infrastructure and to Atlantic Bastion, a Royal Navy effort combining warships, patrol aircraft and autonomous systems against Russian submarines in the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Ukrainian air force says public air raid alert app has been hacked
articles.body:
Ukrainian air force says public air raid alert app has been hacked
KYIV - Ukraine’s air force said on Nov 1 that the public air raid alert app had been hacked.
The app for a short time showed Kyiv and other areas subject to nuclear and chemical alerts and the threat of street combat.
An erroneous message said Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force said on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!”
The abnormality later disappeared.
Ukraine’s Ministry for Digital Transformation said the app was not in operation, but other means of alerting the public were functioning as were air raid sirens.
In a separate event, the mobile app of Russia’s emergencies ministry was hit by a massive cyber attack that resulted in the spread of false information to the public, state news agency TASS quoted the ministry as saying early on Nov 2.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine aid critic set to win Bulgarian presidential election – exit polls
articles.body:
Ukraine aid critic set to win Bulgarian presidential election – exit polls
Acting Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova, backed by the country’s EU-critical government, is projected to defeat pro-Western candidate Andrey Gyurov in the presidential runoff, according to exit polls.
Initial exit polls put Iotova, a critic of military aid to Ukraine, at 50–52% of the vote, compared with 43–44% for Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister.
Iotova thanked voters as well as Prime Minister Rumen Radev and his Progressive Bulgaria party for their support.
“Their vote means a lot, because we will listen to what they have told us,” Iotova said, according to BTA.
“I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Progressive Bulgaria. Mr Radev, we would not have succeeded without you,” she added.
Radev, who took office in May, halted weapons deliveries to Ukraine and withdrew Bulgaria from the so-called coalition of the willing, a group of countries led by Britain and France that have pledged to help provide security guarantees for Ukraine following a potential peace agreement with Russia.
Iotova also argued that military aid would not help end the conflict. “If we pour even more money into Ukraine and deliver new, more sophisticated weapons, this will only lead to further destruction and many deaths on both sides,” she said during a televised debate last week, according to Euronews.
Gyurov, meanwhile, has backed closer security cooperation with Kiev and argued that Russia must end its military offensive before peace negotiations can advance. He accused Moscow of threatening European security while ruling out sending Bulgarian troops to Ukraine.
The elections took place after multiple cargo vessels were struck by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast and several aerial drones entered Bulgarian airspace, incidents Radev described as “absolutely unacceptable.”
Bulgaria summoned a Russian envoy last month following attacks on two commercial ships, one of which sank. Sofia also summoned a Ukrainian envoy in August after a drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, a major energy route linking Russia and the Balkans through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria. The Bulgarian military said the UAV was likely a Ukrainian-made Maya decoy drone.

articles.title: Ukraine suspects nationwide air raid alert app has been hacked
articles.body:
Ukraine suspects nationwide air raid alert app has been hacked
Ukraine's air force said on Sunday that its nationwide air raid alert application had probably been hacked, warning that threat notifications no longer reflected the situation on the ground. The suspected interference came just minutes after the end of a local ceasefire with Russia in the eastern Kherson region.
Ukraine's air force said Sunday it suspected the country's air raid alert system had been hacked.
"The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference," the force said in a message. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Contacted by AFP to establish if the application had been hacked, air force spokesperson Yuriy Ignat said: "Yes, it has been."
The announcement came minutes after the end of the truce between Moscow and Kyiv in the eastern region of Kherson. The localised ceasefire, which started on Tuesday, was the longest of the war.
Read moreCeasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region ends after Russia refuses extension
"Currently, the information broadcast (on this application) about threat levels does not correspond to reality," the Ukrainian Centre for Countering Disinformation warned in a statement.
The app is used across Ukraine to warn people in real time of the threat of air strikes from Russia. People often have only minutes to find shelter in the case of, for example, a ballistic missile attack.
SPRAVDI, Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications, blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
A separate app, which deals specifically with the Ukrainian capital, is still working normally, the Kyiv city authorities said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: IDF again promises drop in reserve duty days in 2027, but security concerns remain
articles.body:
As the academic year begins, the IDF has assessed the expected scope of reserve duty over the coming year as part of a plan to provide benefits and academic accommodations for student reservists. Under the plan, the number of reserve duty days in 2027 is expected to fall by 30% to 40% compared with 2026, depending on security developments and the military's ability to scale back operations. The IDF has already reported a roughly 30% reduction in training exercises and operational deployments planned for December, January and February.
A key consideration in developing the plan was ensuring that reservists would not lose eligibility for benefits simply because they serve fewer days next year. Eligibility thresholds have therefore been adjusted so that those who serve fewer reserve duty days in 2027 than in 2026 can still receive benefits under the established criteria. The military and academic institutions also agreed that degrees earned by reservists who make use of academic accommodations will carry the same standing as any other degree, without distinction or any reduction in academic recognition.
However, promises to reduce annual reserve duty are nothing new. Since the war began, the government and senior defense officials have repeatedly announced plans to cap and significantly reduce the number of reserve duty days required of each reservist, aiming to ease the financial and personal burden of prolonged military service.
Despite efforts to formalize these limits through draft government decisions and legislation, the measures were never finalized or fully implemented. In practice, prolonged operational demands took precedence over the promises. These included the 12-day war against Iran during Operation Rising Lion in June 2025, the continued deployment of forces along the Yellow Line in the Gaza Strip and, later, Operation Roaring Lion against Iran, which lasted more than 40 days.
These operations were compounded by the ground offensive and seizure of territory in southern Lebanon, which began simultaneously in March this year and required a far larger and more sustained deployment of combat troops than originally planned. The IDF continues to maintain a security buffer zone in the area of the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, with troop levels varying according to operational needs.
This security reality has left the same reservists carrying a heavy burden through open-ended emergency call-up orders, known as Tzav 8. As a result, many reservists have continued to receive lengthy mobilization orders that significantly exceeded the service limits they had previously been promised, deepening exhaustion and further eroding trust.

articles.title: Trump, Netanyahu discuss Iran as Tehran reports tanker explosions in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that he had a "very good" conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, with Iran among the topics discussed, as diplomatic efforts continued to avert renewed large-scale fighting between Washington and Tehran.
"Just had a very good talk with him," Trump said, confirming that the two leaders discussed Iran. He provided no further details about the conversation.
The call came as Iran signaled its willingness to pursue diplomacy while warning that it remained prepared for renewed military confrontation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said consultations with mediators were continuing and that the prospects for an agreement depended on Washington's response to Tehran's demands. 
In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi expressed hope that the United States would choose "diplomacy over other paths." He said Iran was prepared for both defense and negotiations, depending on Washington's "rationality."
Araghchi said Saturday that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for discussions on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the United States met several Iranian conditions. He emphasized that no direct negotiations were taking place between Tehran and Washington.
The proposed arrangement would allow shipping through the strategic waterway to resume after Washington fulfilled agreed measures. The strait is a critical route for global oil shipments, and restrictions imposed by Iran have disrupted maritime traffic amid the confrontation with the United States and Israel. 
Iran says two oil tankers exploded after striking mines
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said Sunday that two oil tankers had exploded after striking mines while traveling through what it described as an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels attempting to navigate the strait and has attacked ships it accuses of violating those restrictions. Tehran has sought to strengthen its control over the strategic waterway and use maritime pressure as leverage against Washington. 
The reported explosions underscored the continuing risks to commercial shipping even as diplomatic efforts sought to restore access to the waterway.
Iran designates British military forces terrorist organizations
In a separate development, Iran designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations and declared the country's MI6 foreign intelligence service a hostile entity, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.
Iran's Foreign Ministry accused Britain of supporting U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iranian territory by providing military bases and logistical assistance.
The designation could expose individuals accused of cooperating with MI6 to prosecution under Iranian law and further heighten tensions between Tehran and London. 
The developments highlight the competing diplomatic and military pressures shaping the regional confrontation. While Tehran has indicated that negotiations could lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, reported attacks on commercial vessels and its move against British forces illustrate the potential for further escalation.
No agreement to reopen the strait has been announced, and the outcome of the indirect U.S.-Iran talks remains uncertain.

articles.title: Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
articles.body:
Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants, receives a ceremonial welcome from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and proposes declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction” to develop public infrastructure nationwide, Qazinform News Agency presents its weekly review of Kazakhstan coverage in foreign media.
Euronews: Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a national uranium reserve and faster construction of two nuclear power plants in his annual state-of-the-nation address, Euronews reports.
“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year,” he said, also urging an agreement to advance the Moyynkum project.
Tokayev described an electricity surplus as essential for digitalization and artificial intelligence, while criticizing costly winter electricity imports followed by cheap summer exports.
He also urged Kazakhstan to capitalize on growing demand for overland transport.
“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.
The Aral-Caspian Highway is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by 1,000 kilometres, while the Bakty-Ayagoz railway will add a third crossing with China.
Tokayev designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, prioritizing public infrastructure.
Milliyet: President Erdoğan welcomed President Tokayev of Kazakhstan with an official ceremony
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev with an official ceremony at the Presidential Complex in Ankara before bilateral and delegation-level talks, Milliyet reports.
The ceremony included both countries’ national anthems and a 21-gun salute. Tokayev greeted the guard of honor with “Hello, soldiers.”
According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, the leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional and global issues.
Erdoğan said the two countries would strengthen their enhanced strategic partnership through further cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and the defense industry.
He also pledged close coordination with Kazakhstan during Türkiye’s chairmanship of the Organization of Turkic States.
Erdoğan invited Tokayev to attend the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya and was scheduled to host an official dinner in his honor.
Anadolu Agency: Türkiye, Kazakhstan to deepen defense industry cooperation
According to Anadolu Agency, Türkiye will deepen defense industry cooperation with Kazakhstan through joint production and mutually beneficial partnerships, Turkish defense industry chief Haluk Gorgun said on Wednesday.
His remarks followed talks in Ankara, where President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Gorgun described Türkiye as a reliable, long-term partner offering competitive defense products and policies supporting joint production.
"We will diversify and deepen our areas of cooperation with friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan within the framework of a win-win approach," he said.
He added that combining the two countries’ expertise would contribute to the security and prosperity of the Turkic world.
Hürriyet: Turkic world leaders gather in Ankara for landmark summit
Ankara is hosting the 13th Organization of Turkic States summit on October 29-30 as Türkiye celebrates the republic’s 103rd anniversary, Hürriyet reports.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was the first leader to arrive, receiving a ceremonial welcome from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan before bilateral talks.
Held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action,” the summit will address trade, energy, defense and transport, particularly the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking Asia and Europe.
Türkiye will assume the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan. Leaders are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, appoint a new secretary-general and agree on measures to strengthen cooperation.
Commonspace.eu: Kazakhstan set for major construction program after Tokayev’s speech
According to Commonspace.eu, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction”, calling for new and renovated public infrastructure nationwide.
Priorities include roads, airports, railway stations, housing and healthcare facilities, alongside rehabilitation centers for children with special needs.
Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the “People’s Construction” programme would drive infrastructure development and economic reforms.
“This large-scale project will provide significant momentum for employment growth and improving citizens’ well-being,” he said.
Healthcare Minister Akmaral Alnazarova outlined plans for nearly 70 healthcare facilities, including perinatal centers, children’s hospitals and rehabilitation branches. The projects would add or modernize 9,200 hospital beds.
Euronews: Gold market and central banks: Russia and Kazakhstan sell as Poland and China buy
Kazakhstan plans to reduce gold’s share of its reserves from around 78% to 75% by year-end, after ranking among the world’s biggest buyers in the first eight months of 2026, Euronews reports.
“Kazakhstan has been buying gold for a long time, so it will now be selling at a significant profit,” says Adam Stroniawski, managing director of Polish precious metals dealer Mennica Skarbowa.
He believes the limited reduction and gradual sales will have little impact on global prices. Russia has also reduced its holdings, while Poland continues buying.
AP: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
Kazakhstan is seeking access to both American and Chinese AI ecosystems as rivalry between the two powers puts pressure on countries to choose sides, AP reports.
AI Minister Zhaslan Madiyev joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative in June, and then travelled to Shanghai three weeks later as Kazakhstan became a founding member of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization.
Kazakhstan hopes to attract investment, enter global AI supply chains and influence standards.

articles.title: From fridges to nuclear power plants, hackers are gaining control
articles.body:
In an unstable world super-charged by AI, hacking is the new war front
In the year 2000, on the sleepy banks of the Maroochy River on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a new water treatment facility was experiencing technical difficulties.
Radio communications to wastewater pumps were not working, and the alarms designed to alert staff were not sounding.
Over a three-month period, more than 800,000 litres of untreated sewage was released into local waterways.
At first, council staff attributed the pump malfunctions to growing pains at the new plant.
But the real culprit? A hacker.
In the same year Australia cemented itself on the global stage hosting the first Olympics of the new millennia, it also secured its spot in the world of cybersecurity as the home of the first attributable case of operational technology hacking, becoming a case study used by engineers, academics and governments to this day.
Cyber-retribution a new war front
Operational technology (OT) is the hardware and software that monitors and controls physical machines.
OT is everywhere and is used to operate critical infrastructure such as power plants, conveyor belts, traffic lights, air traffic control systems and water treatment plants.
The Maroochy incident was 26 years ago, but OT hacking is now on the rise and will likely be supercharged by AI.
Last month, hackers remotely raised fridge and freezer temperatures across hundreds of French supermarkets.
In July, 30 water systems across the United States were attacked, consistent with methods used by an Iranian-backed hacking group the CyberAv3ngers.
In June, a cyber security incident brought Australia's second-largest raw sugar producer to a halt, shutting down milling and cane haulage. A Russian-speaking group called The Gentleman claimed responsibility.
In March, the Handala Hack group, also said to be operating under the Iranian government, claimed responsibility for cyber attacks against medical equipment supplier Stryker.
Since US President Donald Trump launched the war in Iran, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued warnings regarding "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber targeting".
In other words: cyber-retribution.
Hacking has become targeted, a new war front for enemies across the globe to attack each other.
The Stryker hack was in retribution for the bombing of an elementary school in southern Iran.
Although the hackers targeted a US company, the attack put Australian hospitals on alert because it remotely wiped associated devices around the world.
Such attacks have obvious financial impacts, but as the technology powering them becomes more sophisticated, the scope and severity of the risks increase.
And as the world destabilises, incentives for hackers to cause harm, including the risk to human life, also increases.
Hacking goes nuclear
In 2025, hackers sponsored by China breached more than 400 agencies across the globe via Microsoft's SharePoint.
One of the agencies was the US National Nuclear Security Administration, the organisation responsible for managing the United States's nuclear stockpile, as well as the nuclear power plants on warships and submarines.
Although an IT hack, not an OT attack, Raji Rajagopalan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, explained that such breaches could be used to conduct an OT hack later.
"They get into a system, lie dormant for a very long time and when there is an opportunity, get into sensitive areas," Dr Rajagopalan said.
"That could create lots of different nuclear incidents that could be really disastrous from a humanitarian perspective."
One protection that nuclear facilities use to prevent such a disaster is an air gap, meaning that administrative systems are largely disconnected from operating systems.
However, Dr Rajagopalan said the assumption that these separations were watertight was not entirely true.
"There are digital upgrades, remote monitoring. All of these always compromise that air gap," she said.
A hacker remotely triggering a nuclear meltdown may sound like the work of Hollywood, but one known incident proved it is closer to reality than fiction.
Stuxnet is a highly sophisticated computer worm.
It was designed as part of Operation Olympic Games, a secret US-Israeli joint cyber-sabotage campaign — although the US government has never publicly taken responsibility.
Stuxnet was unleashed on the Natanz Iranian nuclear facility, where it lay undetected between 2009-2010.
The worm targeted the centrifuges used to enrich uranium, causing them to spin out of control until they broke. It was also sophisticated enough to hide what it was doing.
Stuxnet destroyed at least 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz and set Iran's nuclear program back by about a year.
Such attacks make global headlines when they are discovered, causing policymakers to make sweeping statements at press conferences.
But, Dr Rajagopalan said, political momentum was often lost after the fact.
"Somehow it seems all very theoretical, sounds very futuristic,"
she said.
"You don't want to scare people away, but at the same time, people need to understand that there are consequences to these attacks, that these attacks are real."
Critical infrastructure a sitting duck
Why is OT so vulnerable? How is it that the most critical infrastructure in the world is so at risk of being hacked?
UQ cyber security expert Ryan Ko said the main issue with OT was that much of it had been installed 20 to 30 years ago before existing knowledge of the latest cyber threats.
The old legacy systems were increasingly connected to the internet, he said, and every piece of critical infrastructure connected with OT was at risk.
And with the rise of AI, the scope of cyber-attacks had "changed drastically".
"It is now easier for an adversary to automatically detect a previously unknown vulnerability," Professor Ko said.
OpenAI's rogue agent Medicare data portal hack raised significant alarms for the Australian government.
Although not an OT attack, the incident highlighted how AI can efficiently find weaknesses that in other circumstances could be leveraged by bad faith actors.
Domestically, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) provides frameworks for governments and businesses to boost their cyber-defences against what it has described as "increasingly complex and persistent threats".
"Critical infrastructure and operational technology are attractive targets for state-sponsored cyber actors, cyber criminals and hacktivists," an ASD spokesperson said.
Can we stop OT spiralling out of control?
Dr Rajagopalan said as OT hacking incidents increased, the possibility of inadvertent incidents spiralling out of control also increased.
It is a scenario where neither side may want to engage in "big open-ended conflict, but things going out of control".
In a fracturing world, not only does the current geopolitical climate increase the incentive for enemies to attack one other, but it also limits the ability for allies to work with each other.
"We don't see the major powers coming together, discussing and debating these issues in full earnest,"
she said.
One solution for Australia, Dr Rajagopalan said, could be partnering with multilateral organisations such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations over major powers.
"Bring together smaller groupings of countries who have similar or like-minded interests and who have a certain amount of appeal to international law," she said.

articles.title: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claim to have thwarted advancing Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claim to have thwarted advancing Houthis
Yemen has claimed its army has been able to stop an advance by Houthi militants in the southwest of the country.
The hostilities between Yemen and its coalition allies and the Iranian-backed Ansar Allah movement escalated in September when the Shiite group seized the strategically important Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since also encircled the country’s third-largest city, Taiz, with forces loyal to the internationally recognized government trapped inside.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper, which allegedly has close ties to the Saudi royal family, the Houthis mounted an offensive along the border between Lahij and Taiz governorates on Friday.
However, Saudi-backed troops reportedly pushed back the advancing militants, with airstrikes and artillery fire disrupting the Houthis’ supply lines, and staged a counteroffensive.
Fighting has also continued around the besieged city of Taiz.
Conflicting reports have been coming in regarding the situation in the north of Yemen over the weekend.
On Saturday, the internationally recognized government announced that its troops had recaptured positions in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, which borders Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, in turn, said that they had thwarted advances in the same governorate, as well as in neighboring Marib.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for multiple missile and drone strikes targeting strategic facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the Ras Tanura oil refinery, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, as well as a military installation in Najran region.
In a statement posted on X last Saturday, the Shiite group’s spokesman, Yahya Saree, stressed that the Houthis were conducting such attacks in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen.
Ansar Allah’s representative warned that strikes on Saudi territory would continue until Riyadh ended its “aggression” and lifted a blockade it had imposed on the neighboring country.
After the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, government troops mounted a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Meanwhile, Riyadh has stepped up its air support, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory.
Yemen has remained locked in a civil war since 2014, with the situation further aggravated by a Saudi-led intervention launched the following year. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed government forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.

articles.title: Major fire breaks out at Kstovo oil refinery in Russia after drone attack
articles.body:
Major fire breaks out at Kstovo oil refinery in Russia after drone attack
Drones have attacked the Kstovo oil refinery in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, causing a fire.
Source: Exilenova+ Telegram channel; Russian media outlet ASTRA; Supernova+ Telegram channel
Details: Footage showing a large fire in Kstovo began circulating on social media at around 04:11 this morning. Local residents reported explosions in the city, while monitoring Telegram channels said the Kstovo oil refinery had come under attack, with a major fire breaking out at several locations across the facility.
According to monitoring channels, the drones managed to strike the refinery despite Russian air defence forces having previously repelled attempts to attack the facility.
There have been no official comments from the local authorities so far. It is also unknown what weapons were used in the attack.
In addition, Exilenova+ reported a possible attack on the Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant, which is also located in Kstovo. It supplies energy to local industry, including petrochemical facilities. However, reports that it was hit require separate confirmation.
For reference: The Kstovo oil refinery is one of Russia's largest oil refineries. Its design capacity is around 17 million tonnes of oil per year. By this measure, it ranks fourth among Russian refineries, while it ranks second in terms of motor petrol production.

articles.title: Leader's advisor stresses shift in Iran's retaliation for war
articles.body:
In a Sunday post on his X account, Mohammad Mokhber said Iran is “rapidly” changing its military deterrence strategies to enable it to strike targets far beyond the West Asia region in response to a potential new act of aggression, Press TV reported.
“Of course, the geography of the threat no longer determines the geography of the response,” Mokhber said in the Farsi-language post.
“The redefinition of the scope of deterrence has gone beyond the regional framework, and the origin, scale, and location of a threat no longer impose any limits on Iran’s deterrence calculations,” he said.
The post comes amid concerns that Iran could face a new act of aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime, more than eight months after the two attacked the country without provocation.
Iran responded forcefully to the aggression by attacking targets deep inside the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territories, as well as military bases and assets controlled by the US in regional countries.
The extensive Iranian retaliation forced the US and Israel to end their 39-day aggression in mid-April under a ceasefire brokered by regional countries.
Iran has indicated that it will respond decisively to any new aggression, with military and security officials warning that the scope and scale of its counterattacks will be much greater this time.
On Saturday, Ayatollah Khamenei directed Iran's top military brass to prepare to deliver a swift and powerful response to any threat "without any geographic limitations."
Meanwhile, regional mediators have been trying to work out a diplomatic solution to the Iranian-US standoff, which has disrupted international energy and commodity supply chains.
Iran has indicated that it remains open to such a diplomatic solution if the US accepts its conditions for permanently ending the aggression and lifting its blockades and sanctions against the country.
