articles.title: Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
articles.body:
Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
TEHRAN — Iran has announced reciprocal measures against the United Kingdom, designating its foreign intelligence service, MI6, as a hostile group and its Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations, in response to 'Britain's unlawful and hostile actions against the Islamic Republic.'
In a statement issued on Sunday, November 1, Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the British government's anti-Iranian policies, saying they violated the principles of the United Nations Charter and international law, particularly respect for national sovereignty and the prohibition of unlawful measures against other countries.
The ministry said the measures were intended to safeguard Iran's national security and interests and reaffirmed the government's determination to take all necessary steps to protect the country.
According to the statement, the decision was adopted in response to British actions over the past year, including the country's involvement in the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran through the provision of military bases, facilities and logistical support.
The ministry also cited Britain's decision on July 13, 2026, to bring Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) under the State Threats Act 2026 as part of the grounds for the reciprocal measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the measures were based on a resolution adopted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council and took effect upon publication of the statement on November 1.
Under the decision, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, has been designated a hostile group pursuant to Note 2 of Article 1 of Iran's law on intensifying penalties for espionage and cooperation with the Zionist regime and hostile countries against national security and interests.
The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force, meanwhile, have been placed under Iran's law on reciprocal action against the United States' designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization and will accordingly be recognized as terrorist organizations.
The ministry emphasized that the measures were adopted in accordance with international law and the principle of reciprocity, holding the British government responsible for any consequences arising from its actions.
The decision comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and London over Britain's role in the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran and its subsequent measures against the IRGC.
Iran has consistently maintained that the provision of military facilities and logistical support for attacks against its territory constitutes a violation of its sovereignty and international law. Tehran has also condemned the designation of the IRGC by Western governments as an interference in its internal affairs and a hostile act against the country's national security.
By extending reciprocal measures to British intelligence and military institutions, Iran has signaled that it will respond to actions it considers hostile through its own legal and security framework.
The Foreign Ministry's statement concluded by reiterating that the British government would bear responsibility for the consequences of its policies and actions against Iran.

articles.title: Russia's FSB says minor detained over park attack threat after US tip-off
articles.body:
Russia's FSB says minor detained over park attack threat after US tip-off
Nov 1 - Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Sunday that a Russian minor had been detained over a threat to carry out a terrorist attack in a Moscow park following a tip-off from the United States, news agency Interfax reported.
On Saturday, the FSB said it had received information from the US through established partner channels about preparations for an attack in Moscow and was taking appropriate measures.
The minor had posted photographs of himself on TikTok wearing tactical clothing and a balaclava, holding an object that looked like an automatic weapon, as well as photographs taken at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: "I found a place," Interfax cited the FSB as saying.
"We are grateful to the American side for providing the information," the security service was quoted as saying in its statement.
It said officials searching the minor's home found the clothes and accessories seen in the social media posts, while his phone showed a subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the app Telegram and “a significant number of searches concerning terrorist attacks, mass killings and other acts of violence,” according to Interfax.
Russia's Investigative Committee is considering what legal or procedural action to take, the FSB said.
Tsaritsyno, a palace museum and park complex in southern Moscow, was temporarily closed on Saturday following the US tip-off. REUTERS

Welcome to Your Week in Asia.
Indonesia reports its latest gross domestic product figure as it wrestles with the health and economic impacts of fires and haze, as well as market pressures from a potential MSCI downgrade. The country has also experienced fuel shortages amid the fallout from the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
The U.S. holds midterm elections that are set to have implications for Asia, as voters across the political spectrum have signaled their opposition to the massive data center projects that have boosted Asian tech suppliers' bottom lines. The outcome might also influence U.S.-China relations: While Republicans and Democrats both support Taipei, if the Democrats take over one or both houses of Congress, they could be more eager to pressure U.S. President Donald Trump into moving ahead with a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan.
Get the best of our coverage of Asia and much more by following us on X, where our handle is @NikkeiAsia. We are also on Bluesky with the handle @asia.nikkei.com.
MONDAY
Hong Kong financial leaders summit and Fintech Week
Prominent players in the financial industry and entrepreneurs descend on Hong Kong for a busy week of speeches and networking. Top executives from many of the world's biggest banks and funds are due to attend the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit, which runs roughly in parallel with the city's Fintech Week. Both events come as artificial intelligence poses new risks and opportunities for the sector.
Hong Kong Legal Week
Another event in Hong Kong brings together lawyers, business leaders and policymakers to discuss legal practices and cross-border collaboration. This year's Legal Week will also mark the opening of the first overseas liaison office of the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law (UNIDROIT), a Rome-based intergovernmental organization that studies ways to modernize, harmonize and coordinate private law between states.

TUESDAY
U.S. midterm elections
Americans go to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections to decide whether Democrats or Trump's Republicans will control Congress. If the Democrats win either or both houses of Congress, they are expected to focus on alleged conflicts of interest in critical mineral deals struck by the Trump administration under the banner of building alternative supply chains to China, as well as on trade deals negotiated in the aftermath of the president's "liberation day" tariffs.
Monetary policy: Australia

Singapore bank earnings
Singapore's largest local banks DBS, UOB and OCBC are set to report third quarter earnings results -- starting with UOB on Wednesday and followed by DBS and OCBC on Thursday and Friday, respectively -- as uncertainty mounts over the direction of interest rates. Wealth management has been a driver for the lenders' profitability, although questions abound over whether the trend can be sustained.

Indonesia GDP
Indonesia reports GDP data for the July-September quarter, when there was a sharp increase in natural disasters such as large-scale forest fires and volcanic eruptions, leading to reports of numerous flight delays including to and from Jakarta, raising concerns about economic losses. Capital outflows driven by market uncertainty and the financial environment also remain a cause for concern.
China International Import Expo opens
Shanghai hosts an annual import exhibition, where global companies will showcase new products they aim to sell in the Chinese market. Looming in the background will be concerns about sluggish Chinese consumption and widening trade imbalances, with the world's No. 2 economy on track for another surplus exceeding $1 trillion.
Malaysia monetary policy decision
Bank Negara Malaysia announces its final interest rate decision of the year, with economists divided over whether it will hold at 2.75% or raise borrowing costs. In July 2025, the central bank cut the rate by 0.25 percentage point from 3% and has kept it at the same rate since. New Zealand election
New Zealand holds its general election, with neither the ruling National Party nor the leading opposition Labour Party likely to win a simple majority based on current polling. That could mean the Opportunity Party, a centrist group that has rapidly gained support in the run-up to the vote, could play a decisive role in shaping the next government.
SUNDAY
Vietnam President To Lam visits Japan
Vietnamese President To Lam will make an official visit to Japan through Nov. 11, meeting Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and making a state call on Emperor Naruhito. The visit comes as Hanoi seeks to deepen ties with key economic and security partners, with discussions expected to focus on strengthening the two countries' comprehensive strategic partnership, including in the areas of economic security, trade, investment and technology cooperation. TEHRAN, November 1. /TASS/. Iran has designated the UK’s Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations and has classified the British foreign intelligence service MI6 as a hostile group, the Foreign Ministry said.
According to its statement, "the British foreign intelligence service (MI6) is subject to Note 2 of Article 1 of the law ‘On Tightening Penalties for Espionage and Collaboration with the Zionist Regime and Hostile Countries Against National Security and Interests’ as a hostile group, and the provisions of this law regarding it will apply" as of the publication of the statement.
The document noted that these measures were adopted by the Supreme National Security Council in response to London's hostile actions over the past year, which include participating in the US and Israeli war against Iran by providing bases and facilities on its territory. The document also referenced the July 13 decision to designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC, the elite units of Iran’s armed forces) as a terrorist organization on July 13 under the 2026 Law on State Threats. The ministry emphasized that the UK’s Royal Navy and Royal Air Force fall under the law on retaliatory measures in connection with the US designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization and are, on this basis, considered terrorist entities. The statement stressed that responsibility for the consequences lies with the UK government.

articles.title: Venezuelan army strike on Colombian rebel camp leaves 19 dead
articles.body:
At least 19 people have died following an attack by the Venezuelan armed forces on an encampment belonging to Colombian rebels inside Venezuela, an NGO and sources close to the operation reported.
Juan Francisco Garcia, a coordinator for the human rights NGO FundaRedes, told AFP that Friday's aerial bombing targeting National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels in the border state of Apure resulted in heavy casualties.
Garcia stated that "nine corpses that arrived in San Fernando", the state capital, whilst "another 10 bodies" were transferred subsequently.
Cross-border tensions
The ELN has been the most powerful rebel group in Latin America since the FARC rebel group signed a peace accord with the Bogota government in 2016.
For years, Colombian authorities have accused Caracas of providing shelter and logistical sanctuary to Colombian rebel groups.
The military operation comes while Venezuela remains under sustained diplomatic and economic pressure from Washington, following the United States-backed abduction of former president Nicolas Maduro in January.

articles.title: CAR Army, Russian specialists thwart large-scale operation by radical groups — Touadera
articles.body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. The army of the Central African Republic (CAR) and Russian military specialists thwarted a major operation by a coalition of armed groups in October, delivering a preemptive strike, CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadera said in an interview with TASS.
"It would be premature to speak of stabilization in the definitive sense, and I would not want to engage in wishful thinking. However, let me present the facts as they stand, along with our position on the situation. On October 10, 2026, in the Nabagai-Tissi area of the Vakaga Prefecture, a large-scale operation by a coalition of radical groups was thwarted through the joint efforts of the CAR Defense Forces and Russian military specialists," Touadera said.
He added that the opposing force, numbering approximately 1,300, had planned an offensive against the Vakaga and Bamingui-Bangoran prefectures for the second half of October. A preemptive strike was launched against them. More than 60 militants were neutralized, and a significant quantity of Western-made weaponry was seized. Among those neutralized or forced to flee were several field commanders, including Mahamat Deya and a commander named Khalid from Nourredine Adam's group.

articles.title: Trump says US looking ‘closely’ at report Nvidia CEO is target of China spy plot
articles.body:
Trump says US looking ‘closely’ at report Nvidia CEO is target of China spy plot
- Trump said the US is looking “very closely” at claims that Nvidia chief Jensen Huang was targeted in a Chinese spy plot, after a New York Times report.
- He praised Huang as “brilliant” and said he would likely keep him as an adviser unless evidence showed otherwise.
- China called the report “groundless speculation”, while the case highlights wider US-China tensions over chips, AI policy and Beijing’s tech ambitions.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump voiced on Oct 31 his support for the “brilliant” head of US chip giant Nvidia, Jensen Huang, after a report that he was targeted by a Chinese spy plot.
Trump said the US was looking “very closely” at the issue.
The New York Times reported on Oct 29 that US intelligence officials concluded that a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, who had interacted with Huang, had been funnelling information to Beijing.
China has dismissed the report as “groundless speculation”.
“I have a lot of respect for Jensen. I didn’t know about the specific thing, but I hope he’s going to be OK. He’s a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people,” Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
“We’re going to check it out very closely,” he added.
Asked if he would retain Huang as an adviser, he said: “I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary, I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very above board.”
“But you know, you’re dealing in a very complex issue,” he added.
Huang has advised Trump on AI policy and was among tech CEOs who joined the US leader on his visit to Beijing in May to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Taiwan-born businessman has advocated for the use of his company’s chips in China, where Beijing has been accelerating development of its own semiconductors. AFP

articles.title: Drone strike hits power station in northern Sudan as attacks on energy facilities mount
articles.body:
A drone strike hit a power station in northern Sudan early on Sunday, sparking a fire and triggering loud explosions, witnesses told Anadolu.
The attack targeted the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state, about 334 miles (538 kilometres) north of the capital, Khartoum, according to witnesses.
They said loud explosions were heard around the facility as flames engulfed parts of the station.
Videos circulated by activists on social media showed a large fire at the power station.
The latest strike brought to 12 the number of power stations targeted by drone attacks across six Sudanese states since Monday.
The affected states include Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar, Gedaref, River Nile and Red Sea.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities on the attack or the extent of casualties and damage.
Power infrastructure targeted in series of drone strikes
The latest attack followed another drone strike on Saturday targeting the Hayya power station in Red Sea state, a facility still under construction.
The attacks on power infrastructure come amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The two sides have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements over the integration of the country's military forces escalated into armed conflict.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid a worsening humanitarian and hunger crisis.

articles.title: Matt Canavan enters Capricornia race to set up One Nation showdown
articles.body:
Matt Canavan to run in Capricornia as One Nation's James Ashby withdraws
In short:
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has announced he will nominate for preselection in the Queensland seat of Capricornia.
The seat will be vacated by retiring LNP member Michelle Landry before the next election.
One Nation's party director James Ashby was considering a tilt but has now ruled out running for the seat.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says he wants to run for the seat of Capricornia at the next election.
Senator Canavan confirmed today he would seek preselection for the Central Queensland seat that will be vacated by outgoing Nationals chief whip Michelle Landry.
Officially announcing his nomination alongside Ms Landry on the banks of the Fitzroy River in Queensland, Senator Canavan acknowledged the political risk of switching from the Senate to the lower house.
"My political career may die, but I'm not going to die wondering,"
Senator Canavan said.
After the announcement, One Nation's party director James Ashby ruled out running for the Central Queensland electorate, despite previously considering a tilt at the lower house seat.
Senator Pauline Hanson also said she would not run in Capricornia.
Senator Canavan's bid for the lower house was widely anticipated after the ABC revealed last month Ms Landry's intention to retire ahead of the next election, expected in 2028.
"There's going to be a real fight on for the next election," Senator Canavan told ABC Radio Capricornia today.
Senator Canavan said he needed to "step up" and take a risk by running for the House of Representatives during a "volatile" climate.
"It falls to me," he said after Ms Landry's resignation, adding he "desperately wanted" a change of government.
"I'm happy to sacrifice potentially my own political future to do that," he said.
"I want to be on the front lines with my troops as well. I'm the leader of the Nationals.
"I just have to be there in the trenches with them."
Ashby withdraws
In a statement confirming he would not join the race in Capricornia, Mr Ashby, a close political ally of Senator Hanson and her former chief of staff, said he knew "a number of very worthy contenders" and he would be encouraging them to put up their hands.
"I'll play a role in the campaign here in Capricornia, but my position as national director is one that I take serious; therefore I won't be nominating at pre-selection," Mr Ashby said.
"Capricornia is a seat One Nation can win, so I intend to throw the resources and people behind a strong campaign."
He said the electorate had been "enormously betrayed" by the Coalition in government and in opposition, saying that the mining, agriculture and tourism sectors were suffering.
"Matt Canavan and his colleagues have never shouldered any of the responsibility," he said.
"Until he and the Nationals admit they've been a part of the problem, voters across Capricornia will continue shifting their support to One Nation."
Coalition backs Canavan switch
Senator Canavan, who lives in Yeppoon in the electorate, became the leader of the Nationals in March, replacing David Littleproud, who stepped down.
He currently holds the number two spot on the Liberal National Party of Queensland (LNP) Senate ticket, behind Liberal James McGrath.
A successful move from the Senate to the lower house would shore up the likelihood of Senator Canavan becoming deputy prime minister in a Coalition government, and assure those in the Nationals who hold the view that their leader should sit in the House of Representatives with the other major party leaders.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, when asked if a One Nation surge in popular support was pushing Senator Canavan out of the upper house, declined to comment on the minor party but backed Senator Canavan's bid.
"He's a valued colleague and I'd love to see him in the lower house," Mr Taylor said.
Nationals deputy Bridget McKenzie was asked on ABC Radio National Breakfast if the move was a risk for her Senate colleague.
"In this current political environment there is always a risk running for lower house seats," she said.
"I think Matt's got a great proposition. He has delivered for that community alongside Michelle Landry for a long period of time."
She said One Nation had "made a big song and dance … of wanting to get the PM out of the lodge" and she urged the party to target Labor seats instead of Coalition-held electorates.
Election a 'referendum on net zero'
Senator Canavan said he had been mulling the decision for a while after Ms Landry approached him a few months ago to signal she was considering leaving politics.
He stressed he was nominating for preselection in the seat, which the LNP holds with a 5.8 per cent margin, and was not yet the candidate.
"We're a grassroots party, and whether I'm leader or whatever, I've got to go and present before the Capricornia branch of the LNP and seek their support," he said.
He said the next election would be a "referendum on net zero" and that government needed to "unleash our nation's energy resources again", including coal, oil, gas and uranium.
"We should be building nuclear power stations," he said.
"The way to get cost of living down is to do everything, to build everything, to increase the supply of electricity."
Last year, the Nationals went ahead of their Coalition partners in abandoning their commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050, with the Liberals under then-leader Sussan Ley following.

articles.title: Michigan Democrat’s endorsement of Republican ruffles critical Senate race
articles.body:
By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Layne
ANCHORAGE, Alaska/DETROIT, Nov 1 (Reuters) - A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.
“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.
Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.”
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.
If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda without the aid of Congress.
MICHIGAN RIFT
Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.
“We can’t stand with hate,” Stevens told reporters on Sunday, standing alongside Rogers after the church service.
El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.
Republicans sought to capitalize on Stevens’ move. ”This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of people, it gets dangerous.”
Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.
El-Sayed, who has been subjected to a campaign of racist and Islamophobic attacks, has rejected such accusations and called questions about his loyalty to the United States “shameful.”
He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday, saying he was focused on other issues.
The move appeared to have little effect on some early voters in Michigan, where El-Sayed has a nearly 4-point lead over Rogers, according to the RealClearPolling estimate.
“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.
David Kolar, a 32-year-old elementary teacher, said Stevens’ endorsement “seemed like a last-second distraction.” He said he voted for El-Sayed because of his support for universal government-funded healthcare.
A number of Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to reports from CNN and the Hill.
Stevens’ longtime chief of staff, Justin German, could not immediately be reached to verify the reports, which quoted a statement from him saying, “as of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself.” The statement described him as “shocked and heartbroken” by Stevens’ endorsement.
ALASKA INTERVENTION FALTERS
Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses.
The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the same ballot.
The issue has roiled the campaign over the last several days after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race as a spoiler.
The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.
He joined his party colleagues in accusing the other Sullivan of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.
“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.’”
Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward, Doina Chiacu and David Morgan in Washington, and Nathan Frandino in Anchorage; Additional reporting by Nathan Layne, Laura Matthews, Leah Douglas, Curtis Williams and Mike Scarcella; Writing by Brad Brooks, Andrew Goudsward and David Lawder; Editing by Lincoln Feast, Alex Richardson, Sergio Non, Will Dunham and Deepa Babington)

articles.title: Pope Leo says he hopes Oleshky truce could spur Ukraine-Russia peace efforts
articles.body:
Pope Leo says he hopes Oleshky truce could spur Ukraine-Russia peace efforts
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV said on Nov 1 that he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
Ukraine and Russia said on Oct 23 that they had agreed to a ceasefire in Oleshky, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump with the additional involvement of Pope Leo, to allow aid deliveries and evacuations from the front-line town, which has been suffering from acute food and medicine shortages.
“A humanitarian operation has been carried out to help the civilian population in the city of Oleshky. I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue and lead to fresh concrete initiatives for peace,” Pope Leo said during his Sunday prayer.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said peace negotiators would meet for fresh talks in early November.
Pope Leo spoke to both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky on Oct 16.
Putin told the Pope he supported a Vatican initiative to deliver supplies to civilians in Oleshky and was ready to cooperate, the Kremlin said.
On Oct 27, the Vatican’s foreign minister, Archbishop Paul Gallagher, said that although Leo had recently spoken to Putin and Zelensky, he did not believe the Vatican had played a direct role in arranging the six-day ceasefire. REUTERS

articles.title: Rick Sanchez reports from Alyoshki Russia-Ukraine truce zone (VIDEO)

Rick Sanchez reports from Alyoshki Russia-Ukraine truce zone (VIDEO)
RT’s Rick Sanchez has traveled to the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region to witness firsthand a rare local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine aimed at evacuating civilians and delivering humanitarian aid to residents.
An estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people had been trapped in the town on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, amid Kiev’s repeated drone strikes and the airdropping of mines on supply roads.
More than 750 civilians have since been evacuated under the six-day truce around Alyoshki, arranged with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV. The ceasefire is set to expire on Sunday evening.
Officials from both sides oversaw the evacuations, with civilians offered the choice of relocating to another city in Russia or traveling to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. Evacuees and Russian officials interviewed by RT described months of shortages and the hardships of living under shelling they attributed to Ukrainian forces.
The host of Sanchez Effect compared the town’s destruction to that seen during World War II, pointing to what he described as an extraordinarily high concentration of mines of various types scattered throughout the area.
However, Sanchez expressed cautious optimism as he watched Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova work alongside her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets.
“Could the deal that they worked out for the town of Alyoshki end up being the very thing that sparks some kind of a hopeful sign that maybe both sides can come together in a bigger way?” Sanchez said. He added that some observers believe the truce could pave the way for a broader peace agreement.
Sanchez also suggested that Russia’s drone capabilities may have made Ukraine more willing to “sit down with the Russians.”
Lantratova said she and Lubinets had appealed to Melania Trump to help coordinate further humanitarian missions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that, if successful, the Alyoshki truce could serve as a precedent for future agreements.
